subtopic: VIMY RIDGE SERVICE-REPORTED REFUSAL OF FRANCE TO PARTICIPATE

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of
the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, I address my question to the Prime Minister. It arises out of press reports to the effect that the Republic of France has refused to participate in the guard of honour and other observances at the fiftieth anniversary service at Vimy Ridge on April 9. Will the Prime Minister indicate what explanation there may be for this incomprehensible act on the part of France in view of Canada's tremendous sacrifice, and whether any representations were made to France? It seems impossible to understand why that country would not be represented on an occasion commemorating a battle that helped mark Canada's emergence as a nation and in which Canada poured out its blood and treasure.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: VIMY RIDGE SERVICE-REPORTED REFUSAL OF FRANCE TO PARTICIPATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, preparations for this special Canadian ceremony to mark the fiftieth anniversary of the battle of Vimy Ridge, which is a landmark not only of the war, but, as the right hon. gentleman has said, in our history, are primarily the responsibility of my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I can say that the preparations have been carried out with the full co-operation of
the French authorities. The French government has appointed official representatives both for the ceremony and for the reception of His Royal Highness Prince Philip on his arrival. I believe there are no grounds for suggesting that the French government has not given adequate recognition to this observance.

subtopic: VIMY RIDGE SERVICE-REPORTED REFUSAL OF FRANCE TO PARTICIPATE
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister say why the usual French guard of honour for such events is being denied by that country?

subtopic: VIMY RIDGE SERVICE-REPORTED REFUSAL OF FRANCE TO PARTICIPATE

Mr. Chairman, before launching into the remarks I intend to make on this bill, I should like to answer three questions put to me the other night by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire).
Here is the first. I see the hon. member is absent, but I think Hansard can convey my
April 6, 1967	COMMONS
reply which he will, I am sure, find useful, and can have circulated. It concerned R.O.T.C. pilots who, according to him, would have signed three-year contracts with the government. He accused the Department of National Defence of breaking those contracts unilaterally.
Further to a written request from the hon. member for Lapointe, we gave a reply to the effect that the matter is now under consideration as a result of a new ruling for pilots with a permanent commission. This ruling stipulates compulsory service for five years. As there is no contract but rather what is called a gentleman's agreement between the Department of National Defence and R.O.T.C. pilots, we have withheld a decision to give us time to study the matter. We hope to be in a position to announce our decision in the near future.
The second question concerned the briefs prepared by Mr. Marcel Chaput when he worked for the Defence Research Council. I must say to the hon. member for Lapointe that those reports were brought to the attention of the commission of inquiry on bilingualism and biculturalism but that the latter did not deem it useful to ask us for copies of them.
In the third place, the hon. member for Lapointe asked me a question concerning the use of the French language on Canadian military bases. I must remind him that, on all Canadian bases, administrative and supplementary orders are issued in both languages. Therefore, there is no reason to conclude to any discrimination and the incident he referred to the other night is, if anything, an unfortunate exception.
Mr. Chairman, I should now like to summarize, as succinctly as possible, the position I believe hon. members should take with regard to the issue now before us.
Mr. Chairman, despite the fact that we have been considering this matter quite sporadically for almost five months, I have a feeling that we have not made much progress and that perhaps we are carrying on what I would call a debate by proxy.
It is useful and possibly even essential to have the views expressed before the committee on national defence, in the newspapers and through other media. However, it seems to me that we must be careful not to pose as the spokesmen of the officers now retired or in the armed forces and continue on their behalf, so to speak, a debate which will not
National Defence Act Amendment settle the matter because those officers have taken a position which will surely not change.
Our problem is not to speak for them but to form our own opinion and to reach our own decision.
Mr. Chairman, I am not saying that such evidence is useless; on the contrary, I feel that we must get the gist of it, weigh it, make up our own minds and reach our own decision.
Besides, it is obvious, as shown last night by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso), that some of the evidence, even on the same side, was contradictory and that the same witness managed at times to contradict himself.
Therefore, I would not want us to revert to our starting point and, in addition, to introduce further controversial subjects in the discussion concerning the unification of armed forces. I know that all hon. members who express their views in the house are quite sincere, but I believe there comes a time in a democracy when a consensus must be reached through a vote.
In my opinion, new factors have been introduced in the discussion when reference was made, for instance, to roles or missions. Some people say they are unable to make a decision on such a matter until the roles or missions of the proposed force have been determined.
It would be wonderful indeed, Mr. Chairman, if we could have an instantaneous foreign policy which could be changed from day to day and adapted to our desire to see our country play the role which we believe it is destined to play. But it seems to me that we should believe in our armed forces, in their ability to adapt themselves to these operations or roles which may change eventually.
Having been privileged to work closely with the armed forces in the past two years, I am surprised and even astonished to discover what a store-house of extraordinary talents they are. Let me give as an example the military tattoo.
This is a theatrical performance which is being taken round the country and which I consider to be extraordinary; it was staged entirely by the services. We managed to find in the armed forces people with theatrical experience who were able to produce from scratch a really extraordinary show. All this in my opinion shows the versatility of the officers and soldiers of the Canadian army.

I am also thinking of the contribution to Expo '67 in Montreal, which I find exceptional, made by an officer in the Canadian army, I am referring to Colonel Churchill. His contribution to Expo proved once again that the armed forces are a potential supply of competence. Therefore, when one thinks that the armed forces would be unable to face their role, if changed, one makes an error of judgment.
I wish, Mr. Chairman, to speak very briefly at this stage. I sincerely think that now is the time to determine where we stand and I apologize if, by saying this, I am repetitious. I classified into four groups the circumstances in which we find ourselves:
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)

First, as far as I can see there is nothing that can be added in the way of evidence, facts or figures which has not already been stated. It seems to me that all of the evidence has been given by the minister in the white paper, in his remarks on second reading and by the minister and the military staff before the standing committee. Second, on the other side of the coin those who oppose the concept of unification have been offered every opportunity to make known their views before the committee and through the news media. Third, we have arrived at a crucial point in our deliberations. We can either waste time and go back over the same evidence and testimony again and again with no further progress in sight or, based on all the evidence we have received, we can begin to concentrate on the clauses of the bill now before us.

Fourth, I believe it was the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek who alluded to the fact that most of us have come to some conclusion regarding the merits of this bill. I for one have listened with great interest to all the evidence presented to the standing committee and it seems to me that the reasons

this debate is beginning to become repetitious fall within basic areas. What are those basic areas? What is unification? The minister in tabling the white paper said:
Following the most careful and thoughtful consideration, the government has decided that there is only one adequate solution. It is the integration of the armed forces of Canada under a single chief of defence staff and a single defence staff. This will be the first step toward a single unified defence force for Canada.
On May 28, 1964 the minister said:
So far as the ultimate objective is concerned, this has been clearly stated in the white paper, and I think this is a fair recognition that this is the first step towards a single unified force for Canada.
That was on second reading of the bill. On December 7, 1966, he again devoted many words in explanation of the single service concept. Again on February 7, 1967, at page 440 of the committee proceedings he said:
-a single integrated service encompassing the naval, land, air and support units necessary to carry out its assigned roles and missions and operating under unified management and control.
Here then are four explanations voiced in different words but all meaning the same thing-a single Canadian armad forces rather than three individual services, the army, navy and air force. If there needs to be any further explanation it is set out in clause 2 of the present bill which says:
The Canadian forces are the armed forces of Her Majesty raised by Canada and consist of one service called the Canadian Armed Forces.
Therefore I am satisfied that the goal of one service has been clearly stated and I am sure that all hon. members opposite are fully aware, as I am, that this remains and has been the basic goal ever since it was first announced in the white paper.
What is the purpose of one service rather than three? Like the definition, the purpose has been explained many times before, in the white paper, at various committee hearings, in the minister's comprehensive speech on second reading and on many other occasions. As a matter of fact, there have been so many reasons given for one service I am afraid we are concentrating on each rather than on the raison d'etre itself.
Essentially, as I see it, this can be stated in the following way. All of the members of our Canadian forces, whether combat or support, whether they are in the army, navy, or air force, have one common purpose in respect of which these people can be identified. That is the defence of Canada. Traditionally it has
April 6, 1967

been assumed that to carry out this purpose they must be grouped into three services, one representing the land forces, one representing the sea forces and one representing the air forces.
I can recognize that the overlapping of areas of responsibilities and weapons technology has created grey areas which can no longer be served by the traditional three service concept. We have tried to do something about that. Bill C-90 was the first legislative step required to begin the implementation of a program that would enable us to operate our forces in light of this overlapping of responsibilities by establishing (a) a single chief of defence staff and (b) a single defence staff. The single defence staff was created on a functional basis, that is, personnel, operations, technical services and comptroller general. At the next level commands were reorganized to carry out the following functions: air transport, training, materiel, air defence, maritime and mobile. At the next level the bases were also reorganized along functional lines: transport, operations, administration and supply.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
From July, 1964, to the present we have been integrating our forces to carry out these functions. But because the function-not each individual service-forms the basic criteria for our reorganization, the continuation of a rigid three-service system hinders the full development-

speechtext: Ah.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY. ARMY AND AIF FORCE
speechtext: -and the full benefits that could be gained by a single force.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY. ARMY AND AIF FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the minister answer one question? Can he give me one instance of any evidence given to the committee as to how it hinders at all? Can he give me one word of such evidence given before the committee?

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY. ARMY AND AIF FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would ask my hon. friend to extend to me the courtesy which I extended to him. The hon. member has spoken many times in this debate and I never asked a question with a view to interrupting him.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY. ARMY AND AIF FORCE
speechtext: I am only seeking information, sir.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY. ARMY AND AIF FORCE
speechtext:
Much has been made of the fact that the navy does not have any officer to speak for the navy at defence council. In the functional system which the

National Defence Act Amendment reorganization of the Canadian Armed Forces is bringing about, neither the navy, the army, nor the air force has specific representation at defence council. Instead, the chief of defence staff and the vice chief, together with the chief of technical services, the chief of personnel and the comptroller general as associate members, represent the Canadian Armed Forces. Whether they are army, navy or air force does not matter. They are members of the defence council who represent their functional responsibility and I insist on the word "functional".
Similarly, at the armed forces council there is no specific service representation. The commander of maritime command speaks not for the navy but for maritime command; the commander of training command speaks for his command and not the individual three services which combine to make up his command. Who, then, speaks for the navy, the army, or the air force? The answer is no one, because the traditional three-service concept is redundant in a functional defence system. That is why at this stage in our progress it is necessary to remove the three-service concept and create a single unified force which can operate not as army, navy and air force but as officers and men in training command, in mobile command, in air transport command and in all the other commands or headquarters' functions.
Without going into all the reasons, which are already on the record, I have come to the conclusion that what Canada requires is a single defence force. As I said on February 1 in this house:
This is the crux of the problem. From a single force containing land, sea and air elements, we must be in a position where we can detach the required portions necessary to fulfil a particular commitment. If the particular commitment requires a combination of land and sea elements, or land and tactical air elements, or just a land element we can provide this portion by detaching from the single force the strength and type of force required.
What may be difficult for my hon. friends opposite to understand is that even though there will be no army there will still be soldiers, even though there will be no navy there will still be sailors, and even though there will be no air force there will still be airmen.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY. ARMY AND AIF FORCE
speechtext: How will they know it?

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY. ARMY AND AIF FORCE
speechtext:
Because they will perform the functions. In other words, there will continue to be those who fly aircraft, mariners and warriors. These men, together
14592	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment with those who support them, will not be grouped together in individual services but in one service, the Canadian Armed Forces.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I want to direct the attention of the committee toward a very important fact. For almost five months, in one way or another, there has been a debate on this bill. Either we will have a single unified force or we will not. What has become most upsetting during the past five months is that the service people do not know the outcome. They are most perturbed-

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY. ARMY AND AIF FORCE
speechtext: Who brought it on?

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY. ARMY AND AIF FORCE
speechtext: -that it has taken so long to decide their future course. I agree with them that to extend this period of uncertainty can do nothing but decrease their morale. Whatever period it takes to implement the plans toward the final goal of unification does not concern them. What they want is a decision yes or no. Do we proceed toward unification or not? I think that all the necessary evidence and testimony are now before us.

Allow me to sum up again, Mr. Chairman. Integration established one chief of staff and from that point a single chain of management and command. Because the forces include sailors, soldiers and airmen, and as far as one can see into the future will continue to do so, many have difficulty understanding why we should not continue to have a Royal Canadian Navy, a Canadian Army and a Royal Canadian Air Force. These have been replaced as organizational structures by a single, integrated structure. As a consequence it has now become increasingly difficult to manage personnel on the three-service system, virtually impossible and certainly meaningless to manage finances on that system and, more important, to determine roles and policies on the basis of a three-service division.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
All unification is doing is tailoring the cloth to the developing new organization. The inconsistency between the three-services organization and the present organization causes the shoe to pinch more and more and the point will be reached when the lines of distinction which should be maintained in a three-service organization can no longer be maintained because there will be no sensible way of drawing these lines in the single organizational structure that has now been developed. The only way to overcome this difficulty is to remove the requirement established by law to maintain three services. After this authority has been granted, there will be a great deal of work to be done in terms of amending existing regulations and instructions and it will therefore be some time before the single service can be put into effect.
It is important that this legislation be passed as soon as possible and any lengthy delay would set the stage for a very difficult situation-I believe an unmanageable situation-in the not too distant future. This is not only the course of common sense to enable the orderly progress of the reorganization that was commenced with the legislation that was passed to establish a single chief of staff in 1964 to continue, but it is the only course that will do for our servicemen what they have the right to expect, that is, to establish the fundamental legislative direction and authority to govern the inevitable transition into a single service.
April 6, 1967

At the risk of confusing what I hope has been a simple explanation of the problem, may I add that there will be no difficulty in identifying soldiers, sailors and airmen in the fighting units. It is normal and healthy to expect men in a particular fighting environment to identify with it in some distinguishable way. There is nothing inconsistent in this with a single service. The difference between this and the present system is that it is now necessary to maintain throughout a division between navy, army and air services which is no longer sensible and will become increasingly unworkable.
In conclusion I should like to give a few figures in order to demonstrate that the defence expenditure situation has already been improved by integration. In the way of general background it is perhaps worth noting that the defence expenditures have not varied widely over the last ten years. As a result the proportion of Canada's resources devoted to defence has steadily declined. Expressed as a percentage of G.N.P. the expenditures of the defence department have dropped from about 6 per cent ten years ago to about the current level of 2.7 per cent. This expenditure policy has made it necessary to re-examine continuously defence activities, procurement policies and methods of organization and-operation to find the-economies necessary to offset rising costs. It should also be apparent under these circumstances that every program must be viewed in the light of the resources available and, in particular, its contribution to Canada's defence needs as against that which would result from directing all or part of the resources to other defence programs. For example, if one thinks of buying, on a one-for-one basis, modern warships to replace the 16 frigates that have been taken out of service, -the $800 million or so capital cost plus the continuing operating costs must be considered in the light of what it displaces in the way of other forces.

I thank hon. members for their courtesy. I will not be too long. I have two more pages. This is the real nature of the decisions that have to be made so long as there are strict limits on defence expenditures, as there have been over the last decade.

National Defence Act Amendment
When integration was commenced in 1964 we undertook to manage the defence budget within an escalation not exceeding 2 per cent a year although the actual escalation in salaries and other prices was considerably in excess of this. At the same time we undertook to divert a larger share of the defence budget to capital needs. In the three years, 1964, 1965 and 1966, since this program commenced, defence expenditures have been held within the original targets. Compared with the preceding three years, defence expenditures over this three-year period were reduced by $184 million if the actuarial adjustments to the pension accounts are omitted, and by $158 million if they are included. For comparative purposes it is preferable to omit the actuarial adjustments as the policy of current adjustments to the pension account did not apply throughout the period. By any standard of measurement this is a considerable reduction, particularly when it has been accomplished in the face of rising costs.

I am not trying to hide facts. By way of illustration of rising costs, per capita costs of military personnel were $5,082 per annum in 1961, the first year of the six-year period, and $6,514 in 1966. On the civil side the per capita costs rose during this period from $4,004 to $5,143 and in both cases the major portion of this rise took place in the last three years.
The average military strength in 1963 was 122,700 compared with 105,000 in 1966. The difference, at 1966 per capita rates, amounts to about $115 million per annum. I mention this only to emphasize the problem of coping with rising costs and the compelling need to improve continously our ways of doing the defence business to avoid large increases in the defence budget. We have not managed during this three-year period to meet our original targets for expenditures on equipment. Expenditures on naval equipment in the last three years have been higher than in the previous three years, $208.5 million against $194.4 million, and this has also been the case for army equipment, $120 million against $100.8 million. On the other hand, expenditure on air force equipment have been substantially less. $289.4 million against $507.1 million. The main reason for this is that expenditures in the earlier three year period included $308.2 million for the CF-104 aircraft and there has been no aircraft program in the

National Defence Act Amendment last three years requiring such a large expenditure. The figures I have used will no doubt vary somewhat when the final 1966 figures are in, but not significantly.
It seems to me, then, that the conclusion is clear. Defence expenditures have been reduced, and quite substantially. While equipment expenditures have not been increased as much as we had hoped, they have been increased in the areas where equipment shortages were most acute. As the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre said yesterday, Mr. Chairman, this is my case.

Having heard the remarks just made by the associate minister, Mr. Chairman, I must say that I agree, at least in part, with some of the comments he has made. He stated that the basic questions with which we are faced in this committee are, what is unification and what is its purpose. The associate minister then went on to give his interpretation and his views of unification as well as its purpose. I must say that his observations would seem to be of a rather individual character.
There is one other matter upon which I should like to comment before I get around to the point of examining what unification is and what its purpose is, and that is who developed this plan. This question has been asked on a number of occasions, and I think it is important for the members of the house to know who the author of this plan was. We do not see it being carried out in other countries which are great military powers. We do not see it being carried out in Great Britain. We do not see it being carried out in the United States, France, West Germany or the Soviet Union. Consequently one cannot help but wonder whence comes the idea.
Clearly the idea did not come from the senior officers of the three armed services in view of the large number of retirements, resignations and outright firings that have taken place in that group, somewhat over 40 in all. It clearly did not come from there. In the defence committee General Moncel gave evidence he had prepared four papers on the subject of unification for the minister, but General Moncel was not satisfied with any of them. The minister accepted one of those papers on unification which General Moncel considered was the poorest of the four. I believe this whole question of where this plan comes from is one of the most important questions. Military matters are highly technical and require a great deal of expertise and experience. For these reasons I believe

DEBATES	April 6, 1967
we are entitled to know who thought up this plan. Why is it being pursued now when no other country is pursuing it?
Yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affaires intimated in his customary vague way that he hoped other countries would follow along. The evidence we heard in the committee did not seem to give the slightest indication that any other country was going to do the same thing. It has been stated by the minister and some of his colleagues that the civilian authority must always control the military authority. I believe every one of us would accept that point of view. The only point is that when we are dealing with a highly technical matter such as defence, upon which the whole safety of the country depends, plans which radically change our defence structure should be developed by people who know what they are doing.
We have had no evidence as to where this plan comes from. Indications are that it would seem to come from the minister himself. Perhaps the plan was originated in the cabinet, but we do not know. We would like to know where it comes from. If the plan did originate in the cabinet, the only person who would seem to have any qualifications with regard to military matters would be the Minister of Defence Production who had some senior military experience. There is no one else.
Was this plan thought up by the minister's adviser, Mr. Lee, to whom reference has been made so often? Apparently it has been said that many of the officers and others who are left in the armed services now agree with the plan. Of course, this is probably true because the minister has made it clear that anyone who does not agree with him does not stay in the forces. I would hardly expect any other point of view from the officers who are left. This is one question I would hope the Associate Minister of National Defence might answer before he leaves for Europe this afternoon or perhaps the minister will answer when he returns from his conference in Washington.
I think we are entitled to know who thought up this plan and why it is being pursued, particularly in view of the fact other countries are not pursuing it. There is no evidence that they are going to do so. Most of the senior officers have not recommended it and indeed have spoken against it, with the exception of those who are left in the armed
April 6, 1967	COMMONS
forces. Of course, they are in a rather captive position.
I should like to make one brief quotation from a letter which was reportedly written by Lord Mountbatten to the chairman of the defence committee. The letter appeared in the Ottawa Journal last evening and I should like to quote from the article in that newspaper:
He described himself as "an ardent advocate of unified command and integrated administration of the services."
But he wrote: 'Unified command at the appropriate level is exercised by an officer from any one service, wearing his own uniform and using his own service rank assisted by an integrated staff who commands all units of the three services placed under his command.
I firmly believe that the steps taken in the recent reorganization of the British services are on the right line.
In the British organization care has been taken to preserve esprit de corps and morale and those traditions which help to maintain this in the services and fighting units.
It has been accepted that to achieve this the three services must retain their uniforms and ranks with an identifiable professional head of their service. The idea of a single uniform and rank structure was also rejected as undesirable and unnecessary."
The letter continues:
"The general cut and colour of naval uniforms are internationally so well known that a sailor from any one country can readily be recognized as a sailor in any other country."
These are the views of Lord Mountbatten and they have been promoted by those in favour of unification as an indication that Lord Mountbatten is in favour of unification as envisaged by the government, which he clearly is not.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The next question, to which I hope an answer will be forthcoming sooner or later, is: What is unification? A few moments ago the associate minister attempted to give an explanation. I am glad it is very clear to him because it certainly does not appear to be clear to anybody else, including the former chief of staff who retired only last summer.
I should like to refer to page 2312 of the minutes of evidence of the defence committee, where Air Chief Marshal Miller made the following statement:
I did not know, and I do not know now, the whole answer, all the proposals for unification.
If the chief of staff did not know, then I cannot understand how the associate minister, let alone any of us, knows what it is either.
In this regard I should like to refer to a newspaper which is generally considered one
National Defence Act Amendment of Canada's leading and most thoughtful-the Globe and Mail. The March 22 issue carried an editorial entitled "An Unseemly Rush To What?" The following is an extract from the editorial:
It remains too big a pig-in-a-poke for any parliament to ask Canada to buy, and the commons defence committee, for all its questioning, has not been able to trace out its shape. What is needed is a complete re-examination of the whole defence apparatus, and of the job it is intended to do.
I hope that on another occasion during this debate the associate minister, or the minister himself when he returns, will attempt to give the committee a more lucid explanation of what unification is. As I say, if the former chief of staff was not aware what it was and most of the other senior officers, according to the evidence they gave, did not know or only knew partly what it involved, how can laymen such as the members of this house know?
I now come to the purpose of unification, Mr. Chairman, and certainly this is the $64,000 question. There seems to have been a great deal of difference in the viewpoint not only of members of the house but also of members of the cabinet. The Secretary of State for External Affairs made an interesting but extraordinary speech yesterday which seems to be quite at variance with the evidence given by the present chief of staff, General Allard, as well as with the speech of the associate minister this afternoon. However, as usual the Secretary of State for External Affairs, whose speech I will deal with in detail in a moment, was very careful to make observations which may be taken both ways so that he is fairly well covered in that regard.
As to the purpose of this new unified force, as it is called, we were told by the minister, as well as by his colleagues both inside and outside the house, that one of the advantages of unification would be that it would be cheaper and more economic. That is certainly an important consideration, as everyone would agree.
This afternoon the associate minister gave us the most extraordinary set of statistics. It is often said that statistics can prove almost anything, which reminds me of the statistician who was six feet tall and drowned in a river with an average depth of two feet. The fact remains that we were told that unification would bring about economies and reduce defence costs.
A few moments ago the associate minister indicated that we would now be spending a
14596	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment smaller proportion of our gross national product on defence than was the case previously, that there would be economies. This is an interesting way of looking at the subject, but the fact remains that according to the defence estimates for the coming year, which the house will recall from previous discussion were compiled as if the bill had already been passed, defence expenditures this year are some $115 million more than they were last year. One of my hon. friends on the government side of the house has indicated that we are certainly going to save money with unification.

The hon. member for Leeds says that that is right. It may be true, but I would suggest it is a strange way to try to convince the public we are going to save a lot of money and reduce expenses by unifying the forces when we have no way of proving this. The only thing we do know for certain is that it will cost over $100 million a year more to start with, though some of the evidence given in the defence committee indicated that it will cost even more. Although I realize that expenditure is important, it is not of prime importance when we are dealing with matters which affect the future safety of this country. In such case cost itself is not an overriding consideration.
The next question is: What is this unified force going to do? There seems to be a great difference of opinion on this score. Since defence is interrelated very closely with foreign affairs and foreign policy, as everyone agrees, we have to look to foreign policy to see how we should design our defence forces.
Yesterday afternoon the Secretary of State for External Affairs made a very long and interesting speech on foreign affairs and he reiterated Canada's foreign policy. I listened very carefully to the minister's speech and I reread it this morning. There is nothing in his speech vis-a-vis foreign policy with which I disagree. I thoroughly agree with his enunciation of our foreign policy. However, toward the end of his speech the Secretary of State for External Affairs stated-words to this effect are to be found at other places in his speech-as reported at page 14567 of yesterday's Hansard:
Indeed, it-
That is the unified force.
-will be capable of performing the same variety of roles required now by our foreign policy commitments and, in my view, performing them much more effectively.

DEBATES	April 6, 1967
I am glad to hear that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is so well assured in that regard, because he did not give one shred of evidence to support his view to this effect. Indeed, just the opposite: he admitted the increasing danger of nuclear submarines sent out to sea by the Soviet Union.
Our naval capabilities are now less than they were but the minister failed to explain why we are unable to man some of our ships. The new ones supposed to be laid down have not been laid down. How can we carry out our defence commitments vis-a-vis the navy in view of the increasing submarine danger? The minister had some sort of answer to this, and as reported at the bottom of page 14563 he said:
In addition to the bomber and the I.C.B.M. threat there is a growing threat to this continent, which obviously we cannot ignore, from submarines. This was pointed out by the hon. gentleman who spoke a few moments ago. In answer to what he said I would point out that we are co-operating with the United States to meet this threat, not only as a matter of continental defence but also within the NATO framework.

As he frequently does, the Secretary of State for External Affairs got around this particular argument in a nebulous way by saying that we are working in co-operation with our allies. I think it is clear, since our naval forces do not now have the capability they had several years ago, that our allies, particularly the United States, are taking over this function to an increasing degree.
I now wish to ask a question bearing on our improved military capability. The Secretary of State for External Affairs told us yesterday that in his opinion he was sure it would improve. I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs this question, and I am sure it will be referred to him by others. Has he ever discussed this matter with Air Chief Marshal Miller or with General Allard? Certainly the Prime Minister did not discuss it with Air Chief Marshal Miller and if the Secretary of State for External Affairs did so I should like to know.
In any event, referring again to the testimony of the former chief of staff who retired last summer I point out that he said he saw no significant financial or military advantage in unification over integration. Are we to ignore the expertise of the chief of staff appointed by the present Minister of National Defence, are we to ignore Air Chief Marshal Miller's great knowledge and accept statements of laymen in this matter such as the
April 6. 1967	COMMONS
Secretary of State for External Affairs, admittedly a layman, or the Minister of National Defence? If the air chief marshal said there was no financial or military advantage in unification, why are we doing it? I should like to know. The associate minister seems quite sure in his own mind; he is satisfied with this measure. I am not, and I think many other hon. members are not satisfied.
For the past few months it has been strongly hinted that the purpose of this new force is really to perform only some sort of peacekeeping operation on behalf of the United Nations. In some remarks I made on January 31 last I quoted from an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen last year-I do not want to take the time of the committee to quote it again-pointing this out. As hon. members know, the Ottawa Citizen is generally considered by most people to be the leading spokesman for the government, for various reasons. If the Ottawa Citizen said this I do not see how we can very well ignore it. Other newspapers have said this, including the Globe and Mail, which until recently had a pipe line to government intentions. That pipe line seems to have been ruptured within the last few days. In an editorial of March 22 last, to which I have already referred, the Globe and Mail said:
A Defence Department that is creating a unified force which could not deal with these present commitments anyway and which seems wholly designed to undertake international peace-keeping interventions which the world has not asked Canada to undertake and which Canada's External Affairs Department has not said that Canada will undertake.
This makes the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs yesterday very interesting because he made it very clear, which is saying something, that Canada's basic commitments were for the defence of Canada through collective agreements, including the defence of our coastal waterways, that we are still keeping our commitments to NATO, NORAD and the rest, and that we would like to be able to meet requests from the United Nations. The Secretary of State for External Affairs made it clear that our international commitments as outlined by him had not changed. Then why are there these other suggestions?
In this regard I think the most important observation comes from the present chief of staff, General Allard, who made the following statement when testifying before the defence committee:
-Canada now wants-while remaining faithful to its existing commitments-to decide itself on the
National Defence Act Amendment
part it wishes to play in the new international society-this is not only its right-it is also its duty. It is its duty to participate, to the best of its ability-in keeping the peace by supporting the organization which has made itself the champion of the smaller nations-the United Nations Organization.
In short, that is the transformation proposed by the white paper. That is what we are trying to do. My duty is to organize the military forces in accordance with government policy.
That statement, perfectly simple, perfectly straightforward, is completely at variance with the statement of intention made yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. With conflicting evidence as to the purpose of the force, what are we in this house to do? Where are we going? What is this for?
General Allard, the chief of staff, says one thing. The Ottawa Citizen and the Globe and Mail agree with him. The Secretary of State for External Affairs says another thing. In fact, he refuted strongly the idea that Canada should take up only a peace-keeping role, implying that that was a cloud nine idea and thereby taking a slight crack at his friends in the New Democratic Party who do not think it is a cloud nine idea.

It seems that there is much difference of opinion about the purpose of this force. Is it to be solely for United Nations peace-keeping or will it be used for our regular commitments? If it is for our regular commitments I point out that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has suggested how we can integrate this force with the forces of our NATO allies in Germany, in NORAD and the like. Evidence given before the defence committee showed that integrating this new force with the existing forces of our allies is like trying to mix oil and water. It will not work. So I ask, what is all this for? I think we are entitled to a much better explanation than we have had to date about this matter. It is very disturbing indeed.
If the force is to be used only for peacekeeping purposes and we let the United States look after the defence of North America completely, where does that leave
14598	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment us? Will we end up with this country being partially occupied by United States forces? Is that in accordance with present day Canadian nationalism? I think not. If we become nothing but a military province of the United States, this lovely peace-keeping force we are arranging would never be used. The United Nations would never dare to use it because it would be thought that it was some sort of quasi-United States or United States influenced organization. We would be in the position, as the right hon. Leader of the Opposition said, of being all dressed up and having no place to go.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
We need a great deal more clarification of some of these matters before this bill is decided. The associate minister has told us this issue must be decided quickly before any more questions are asked. Well, some fundamental and basic questions have not yet been answered and I think it is up to the government to give us the information required. Otherwise the only conclusion reasonable people can draw is either that the government is attempting to deceive this house and the public as to the real reasons for unification or, as is so often the case, the government does not know where it is going. In an apparent attempt to contribute to cabinet solidarity the Secretary of State for External Affairs told us yesterday that he thoroughly believes this unifying force will enable us to meet our present commitments more efficiently. He expressed this view even though the evidence of all those who possess expertise on the subject is to the contrary. We should like some clarification of these matters and I hope it will be forthcoming before the present debate is terminated.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Oxford has indicated that before clause 2 passes a lot more clarification is needed. The note I would stress in the course of my few remarks this afternoon is: "Let us get on with it." I refer to an editorial under that title written by service people in the publication Voxair which is put out by the Canadian forces base at Winnipeg. It begins:
The integration process began two years ago and that, to the rank and file, seems a long time.
I would point out that this editorial was written on August 19, 1966. It says that servicemen find it hard to understand the reason for the slow rate of progress, and goes on:
More difficult to comprehend is the opinion, often expressed in the recent controversy, that the integration process is too fast...

DEBATES	April G, 1967
Most proponents of the "too fast" idea appear to be those who were against integration in the first place and who believed that integration and unification would not become a reality. When it now appears that it will, the natural reaction for anyone resisting change must be to attempt to delay the change.
Later in this editorial, which is in strong terms, the editor writes:
Integration appears slow to those in the field. This should make a good argument for speeding up the process as much as possible. Any change of the magnitude of the one undertaken is difficult and sometimes painful, but the quicker we complete the change, the less painful it is going to be. If, on the other hand, the phase of change is allowed to go on ad infinitum we can be certain that morale will be adversely affected.
The concluding words of the editorial which, as I say, was written on August 19, 1966, are:
It was known before the start that this was a difficult undertaking, but the over-all gains clearly justified the decision to go ahead. Now, in the middle of the changeover, let's not procrastinate for reasons of doubtful validity, but let's get on with it.

I think that no one travelling in a bomber across the ocean could hope for a more delightful travelling companion than the hon. member. I wish we could go together again soon.
My hon. friend referred yesterday to the events which took place at Vimy. When we reflect on what happened there half a century ago we think of the colossal wastage of human life that occurred there which, as at Verdun, destroyed a generation. We think of the Somme, of Passchendaele, of the tremendous loss of life which occurred in those battles and their lasting effect on Britain, France and the dominions.
I visited Vimy with some emotion because the name of one of the members of my own family is on the memorial there. Referring to the events of April 9, 1917, Gregory Clark had this to say, writing in Weekend Magazine of April 1:
At 5.30 a.m., April 9, in a sleet and snow blizzard, the volcano of our artillery erupted.
Behind the wall of fire we floundered up the ruined and filthy slope.
We took the Ridge. In the next three days we went 4,500 yards, took 4,000 prisoners, 54 cannon, 104 trench mortars, 124 machine guns.
We lost 3,598 killed and more than 7,000 wounded.
The author concludes: "Symbols are costly".
I have visited many of the battlefields of Europe and several in Asia. I really do believe that progress in military expertise, in tactics and in strategy has been phenomenal.
23033-923J
National Defence Act Amendment I was with Colonel Fane, if I may call him that, going over some of the ground of the first world war, and I like to believe that there has been definite progress in the arts of war designed to reduce human slaughter and yet to accomplish those things which are intended to preserve peace and liberty.
In this regard I would call attention to some things which were said by General Worthington. "Worthy" was assistant adjutant and quartermaster general at national defence headquarters. A dynamic personality in every appointment, he became the revered and gallant commander of the 4th Armoured Division in 1942 and commander in chief of the Pacific command in 1945. Just think of some of the personalities with whom he was associated-men like Admiral Halsey and others of that calibre who were among the most outstanding military leaders of that decade. General Worthington showed his imagination and his managerial talents as coordinator of civil defence for Canada in the years from 1948 to 1957. Some of the things this great Canadian did in those years in a field which was of little interest to most people showed how truly knowledgeable he was.
I feel it would be useful at this point to refer to an article written by General Worthington under the heading "Reorganization Of The Armed Forces Long Overdue". This appeared in the Ottawa Journal of Tuesday, April 4, 1967. The general said:
In February and March the parliamentary defence committee sat for six weeks hearing 23 high-level military "experts" on the integration and unification of Canada's armed forces.
The testimony of most of these experts had a disturbingly familiar theme:	What was good
enough for the last war will be good enough for the next.
As one of Canada's oldest generals it is my opinion that at the end of any large war the existing generals should be thanked, decorated and pensioned off.
Put up statues, if you like, but don't let the old brigade meddle with the future organization of the services. Hand that responsibility over to the young, fighting colonels who had to fight the war with the existing weapons.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Almost invariably the senior commanders plan with their heads looking over their shoulders back to the time when they were young and trained on equipment and tactics of that day.
General Worthington warns us of the peril at this time of thinking backward which could result in annihilation. He says:
I believe the present reorganization of our armed forces is long overdue. It indicates up-to-date planning and foresight as opposed to prejudice,, obsolescence and nostalgia.
April 6, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment
He points out that Canada's military personnel could be wiped out in a single battle. I consider that significant because when we look at the statistics of Canada's defence effort we notice that currently we are spending approximately $1.6 billion. I feel that the Associate Minister of National Defence only started to put on the record the broad line of economies which have been effected. There could have been several speeches on this aspect alone had it been felt desirable to make them.
Had we never intended to change or modernize anything but merely replace the proper modern materiel for our existing establishments, this alone would cost many hundreds of millions of dollars. I believe I am correct in saying that the utilization for defence purposes of only 2.7 per cent of the gross national product of a country such as Canada places us in the category of being the third lowest contributor to the NATO alliance. Countries such as the United States, which comparatively have an immensely larger gross national product, are making much higher contributions. The point is that we in Canada are not making large contributions on the basis of our wealth and general economic strength. In terms of people we actually have a little over 100,000 men, sailors, soldiers and airmen, and this very fact alone at this time happens to be most helpful to us in the engineering of new processes, of new experimentation and in the pragmatic effort of bringing into being a concept which has been anticipated in every serious military school in the world, in the Soviet, in the United States, and all through Europe.
General Worthington said:
Any suggestion that we provide defence for Canada alone is a ludicrous myth.
We are not in the stand on guard era any more with regard to Canada against an American enemy. If that is our thinking, then we should do it with splendour and simply multiply the kind of exercise performed at Fort Frontenac where we have ceremonials which I watch each year. They are decorative but neither practical nor very real.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs made an important contribution to the debate when he reminded us that our defence responsibilities are in the new collective sense and not in the isolationist or independent sense. I think he brought into proper balance our responsibility to NORAD, a contract that was entered into by the previous administration, and to NATO, which responsibility we


assumed under the leadership of the late Louis St. Laurent, and to the United Nations.
General Worthington continues by saying:
But Canada can produce a new, compact, efficient and integrated force to meet the challenges of the future. This force would be a highly skilled fighting machine, mobile and flexible, with an understanding of land, sea and air combat.
When we discuss mobility I am reminded of General Macklin who some people characterize as the author of mobility. I think it a fact that when we sent a mobile force to Suez some years go we had to dismantle our one capital ship in order to put our so called mobile force ashore. This is incredible. I believe that if Canadians generally could have sat in on some of the hearings of the national defence committee, especially when we were privileged to visit mobile command-at that time as I recall it was under the command of General Allard-they would have been impressed with the step-up that has been achieved in communications.
It would almost seem that many of the military concepts which were familiar to people as recently as the 1950's now tend to be somewhat obsolete. We are moving at a rapid pace. Frankly, I was impressed with certain parts of the evidence given by Air Chief Marshal Miller. I thought he was right when he spoke in terms of the pragmatic effort in what we are doing and the fact that this never can be achieved overnight. The Minister of National Defence has made this point more than once. This is something which never will be finalized. Certainly it will take a period of years to bring about a high degree of perfection. I believe at one point he suggested it might be something like seven years before unification can be finalized. Air Chief Marshal Miller stressed the fact, which was emphasized by the Secretary of State for External Affairs yesterday, that the interrelationship between defence policy and foreign policy is like the chicken and the egg in that defence policy really carries out or supports foreign policy.
If I wished to be frivolous I could pull out a quotation of Mao Tse-tung to almost the same effect, except that he considers war to be an extension of politics. I like to think that we are doing it in the reverse and that basically what Canadians are concerned about is to develop a military policy to protect and enlarge peace.
In his remarks the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, I thought very appropriately, mentioned Somalia. Perhaps this is the best example of a potential danger area. Here
April 6. 1967	COMMONS
we have Somalia occupying a strategic part of Africa. Berbera looks across the Gulf of Aden to the British base of Aden which once dominated these waters. Britain plans to pull out of Aden next year. Many of us have had discussions with people who know something about this situation. At the moment Russia is moving into Somalia and is providing 150 Mig fighter bombers and enough T-34 tanks for an armoured brigade. This is just a little country. Egypt and Algeria present special and disturbing problems, as well as Syria and Iraq.
This is a current topic in world news. It is a frightening commentary that little Syria can bring war to her neighbours, Lebanon and Jordan, and from this area to the world. Many military prophets have suggested it is from the Middle East that there could develop a conflagration. Looking at these disturbing patterns we see, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Defence have previously indicated, that Canada has an important role in these areas of operation. I do not like to call them policing operations but in some places that is what they are. However, in other areas these operations require as much valour and far more imagination than was demonstrated in the battles of Passchendaele. So I think we must venture into the future with courage and great imagination.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
A few days ago I was in Jakarta and spent some time talking to friends who explained to me why Russian tanks were patrolling the streets. They told me that under President Sukarno that little country-perhaps I should not say little because it has a population of 110 million but it is little in the sense of wealth as we know it today-actually beggared itself to the extent of $2 billion for Russian armament. This presented a tremendous problem which happily has been resolved as a result of political developments.
If this House of Commons has the courage, and this proposal calls for a special form of courage and a certain quality of faith, we propose to venture into new concepts in the military field just as we have done in a variety of economic areas.
Just think, Mr. Chairman, of the imagination that was demonstrated in this country when the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National decided to institute the piggyback system. This disturbed many existing concepts. Think of the results in Canada from the
National Defence Act Amendment coast to coast large scale suburban development and urban redevelopment when many of the old lines of demarcation and boundaries were struck out in the interests of people and real social objectives. In the words of Air Chief Marshal Miller, the only approach that could be taken was the pragmatic approach. But let us move decisively toward that objective. We are not sure just how it will be accomplished or how soon, but we must not box ourselves in by fixing rigid lines in every area.
Let us reflect on the difficulties of the Canada-United States auto treaty in respect of which we all share a burden of responsibility and pride in this parliament. We do not know where it is going to lead us exactly but we think it will lead to progress for Canadian workers and the Canadian people.
Let us consider the great contribution of Colonel Ed Churchill mentioned by the associate minister a few minutes ago with respect of Expo. The whole idea of Expo came from the previous administration. This was an adventure in faith. Many of us have gone down to Montreal by helicopter, by ship, or by car to look at St. Helens Island and we all remember what a mess it was just a few months ago and how hopeless the whole thing looked. Yet through co-operation on the part of various agencies of government, the private and public sectors of our economy, industry and labour with its various skills, together with the co-operation of many nations, this great international complex has come into being.
Let us think of what has happened in the whole area of communications. We have moved rapidly from the telephone and wireless to radio, to Telex, to television, and to Telstar. All the old boundaries and ideas had to be stripped away and replaced.
I have been told abroad that many countries are looking at our act of faith in respect of unification with increasing interest because they know our military purpose and that purpose is peace. In addition, for the very reason indicated by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre the past performance of Canadians in stormy places like Vimy, Passchendaele and the Somme has proven that we do not intend to welsh out of our responsibilities. We are not trying to pull out of NATO or to get out of our responsibilities to the United Nations or to our good neighbour on this continent. Whatever we do in the
14602	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment military field our purpose is to preserve liberty and peace for all men. That is our approach and we are trying to carry out this obligation wisely and with imagination.
Let me repeat the plea of my distinguished colleague, the Associate Minister of National Defence, and the requests of servicemen over some considerable period of time: let us get on with the job together.

Before commencing I should like to say I am happy to be able to commend the hon. member for Leeds who is one member on the government side who has made his own speech rather than read one prepared by a member of the staff of the minister or the associate minister.
I am pleased to know that the associate minister is going overseas as a representative of Canada at the fiftieth anniversary celebrations of the battle of Vimy Ridge. Presumably the part you read was the part I did not like. I very much regret that because of previous commitments I am not able to accept the invitation of the Minister of Veterans Affairs to attend those celebrations. I happen to be one of the individuals described by the deputy minister in a letter written for the minister. The thought expressed in that letter is very nice in that it suggests that medical care should be provided for the 73 veterans who are being taken to Vimy Ridge to represent their battalions.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
He felt that this extra precaution was necessary in view of the quite advanced age and rather frail health of many of those who will be making the trip. Of course this does not apply to me. Being one of the possibles, I would have liked to be there. I would have liked very much to have the opportunity to accompany the associate minister because I might have been able to discuss with him some things about defence and perhaps show him why it is that people like me, whose service in Canada's army was very long, although perhaps not as illustrious as some-

-are opposed to the total unification of Canada's armed forces. I am opposed to it not because I am a member of the opposition and not because I belong to the Conservative party; if I were a Liberal and on the government side of the house I would still oppose it because of my personal convictions.
I believe this attitude holds good for the members of this party. We do not go all out for the total unification of Canada's three armed services. We think it is a wrong step. We think it should not be made at this time. We believe that the process of integration of the senior echelons of the services is adequate at this time. That is a view I have held for almost 50 years. I do not think anybody can say that my views are political. Fifty years ago I was not very politically inclined even though I started voting when I was 18 years of age because I happened to be in the army at that time. I very strongly resent the statements made by some hon. members on the government side that the opposition to this bill is entirely for political reasons. I do not believe that is so. It amazes me more than I
April 6, 1967	COMMONS
can tell you that 100 per cent of the Liberal members can vote for this bill. It is entirely beyond my understanding how they can support it.
I sometimes wonder from whom the minister is taking his orders. He is so extremely adamant in his support of his bill. We cannot change his mind at all. He will not listen to reason. He simply will not deviate one iota from the ideas that he set forth in the original draft of the bill. True, there have been a few small changes made, but they do not amount to very much. Many people are blaming the minister and only the minister. That is not the way I see it. The minister is merely the member of the government who is spearheading this legislation and trying to get the bill through parliament. He cannot do it without the support of every member of his party in the house and without the full support of the rest of the cabinet, including the Prime Minister. So, any blame that is placed on the minister must be placed equally on all the other ministers, the Prime Minister and every member of the Liberal party in the house.

speechtext: Everyone?

speechtext:
Everyone. Nobody in that party voted against the bill at any time. I think it was the hon. member for Lambton West, who has just come into the chamber, who remarked that the committee did not assume political implications until the hon. member for Cape Breton South was made a member of the committee in my place. I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that from my observations the committee became political a long time before the hon. member for Cape Breton South was made a member of it. I had to give up my place on the committee not because I was too quiet or for any reason like that but because of commitments in other places which I had to carry out.
The biggest trouble this bill has encountered has resulted from its presentation by the minister. The minister has made statements which have had to be somewhat modified at times, but the first statement that got him into trouble was his explanation of unification. I should like to read the definition that the minister gave on December 7, 1966. He had said this before. I quote from page 37 of a copy of the speech the minister made in the house on December 7 last:
Unification is the end objective of a logical and evolutionary progression.
What in the name of heaven does that mean? On page 59 of the same speech, the
National Defence Act Amendment second paragraph, he made a statement which has probably got him into more trouble than his explanation of unification. He said:
Although a unified personnel management system will be introduced, the separate units and elements of naval, field and air forces will continue to exist.
Now comes the important part:
That is to say, while the barriers to movement of personnel between the forces will be removed, personnel in the combat forces will continue to be identified as sailors, soldiers and airmen until the force structure within the unified force is developed.
Isn't that a dandy?
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
They will continue to be identified as sailors, soldiers and airmen until-
Note the "until"
-the force structure within the unified force is developed.
A statement like that would get anybody into trouble. I wonder whether he read it before he made it in the House of Commons.
Those are the things that have caused trouble for this bill. In the defence committee on February 7 he changed his statements a little.
I quote from page 440 of proceedings of the committee No. 14 where he said:
When I refer to a unified force I refer to a single integrated service encompassing the naval, land, air and support units necessary to carry out its assigned roles and missions and operating under unified management and control.
What does that tell us? Not very much more. It makes one wonder just exactly what is going on in the mind of the government, in the mind of the Prime Minister and in the mind of the Minister of National Defence. Until today I have liked to think that the Associate Minister of National Defence was not quite in accord with everything that was going on. I had hopes for him. I would still have hopes for him if I were only able to go with him to Paris tomorrow as I had the opportunity of doing.
We have been briefed by a number of very able and noted former servicemen. We were briefed by a few who were still serving, such as Air Marshal Sharp, Air Marshal Reyno and Major General M. R. Dare, who is the deputy chief of reserves and a long time friend and associate of mine in whom I have great faith. We were also briefed by Brigadier Lawson, judge advocate general. A number of ex-officers who belong to the Tri-Service Identities Organization also appeared before us. We also had before us the chairman of the
April 6. 1967

National Defence Act Amendment committee on the maritime component of the Canadian defence forces, the president of the Naval Officers Associations of Canada, Mr. Wilson, and the president and vice president of the Ontario division of the Navy League of Canada. We were briefed also by the president of the Toronto branch of the Naval Officers' Associations of Canada.
I will list the very senior and experienced officers who have seen very responsible service in the past and briefed members of the committee. They were headed by Rear Admiral Brock, Rear Admiral Dillon, Rear Admiral Landymore, General Foulkes, Mr. Patrick, Lieutenant General Moncel, Air Marshal Annis, Air Vice Marshal Hendrick, Lieutenant General Fleury, General Allard, who is still serving as the chief of the defence staff, Vice Admiral Rayner, Air Marshal Curtis, Lieutenant General Guy Simonds, and Air Chief Marshal Miller. The majority of these people who are not serving now were against the total unification of Canada's armed services. They have the same attitude that I have, and it is not because we are old fogeys or are living in the past. These men are mostly young men who have just been retired before completing their normal term of service.
There are a number of things that I simply cannot understand. For example, how in the name of heaven are the Canadian armed forces going to operate with one rank structure? It is difficult to imagine a lieutenant colonel commanding a ship or an admiral being a lieutenant general. It is not so difficult for the air force to conform to the new rank structure because before their present rank structure they had army ranks and army uniforms.
The provision of a single uniform for Canada's defence forces seems to me to be a little out of line. No less a person than Admiral Lord Louis Mountbatten said the same thing as reported first in the Victoria Colonist of April 4, I believe, and in the Ottawa Journal of April 5. Incidentally, his letter was written to and published by the brother of the former chairman of the defence committee. The article reads as follows:
Lord Louis, in the letter to Commodore Groos, said he hoped to clarify previous statements. He described himself as "an ardent advocate of unified command and integrated administration of the services".
I agree with that. It continues:
But he wrote: "Unified command at the appropriate level is exercised by an officer from any one service, wearing his own uniform and using
[Mr. Fane.)
his own service rank assisted by an integrated staff who commands all units of the three services placed under his command.
I firmly believe that the steps taken in the recent reorganization of the British services are on the right line.
In the British organization care has been taken to preserve esprit de corps and morale and those traditions which help to maintain this in the services and fighting units.
It has been accepted that to achieve this the three services must retain their uniforms and ranks with an identifiable professional head of their service. The idea of a single uniform and rank structure was also rejected as undesirable and unnecessary."
The letter continues:
"The general cut and colour of naval uniforms are internationally so well known that a sailor from any one country can readily be recognized as a sailor in any other country.
Sailors the world over take great pride in this and so in their own services do soldiers and airmen."
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I subscribe to that view very strongly, as I have said at other times in this house. My time is going quickly, unfortunately, but I wonder what the minister is trying to do to Canada's armed services. I wish he were here today to listen to what I have to say about him, because it is what I believe and what I have been told many times back on the prairies where people are credited with not showing too much interest in this debate.
In Alberta, the people say, "This man Hellyer, what about him?" He was a corporal and we know the record concerning two other corporals who had ambitions. Corporal Bonaparte took the name of Napoleon and as a result of his ambition he ruined the flower of France's manhood at the time he was running the affairs of that country. He jumped from a corporal to a field marshal. We also have the recent example of Corporal Schickl-gruber who took the name of Hitler. He ruined Germany. He jumped from a corporal to commander in chief of the forces and ruler of the nation.
Today we have ex-Corporal Hellyer who is trying to do the same thing but he is trying to do it legally by having this bill approved by parliament. At this time may I read a little item from B. H. Liddell Hart's book, "The Other Side Of The Hill." The author sets forth the views of some of the German people about their leader, Hitler.
He (Hitler) would not believe what he did not want to believe.
Is there not a parallel there with our minister? The author states that General Jodi had
April 6, 1967

come to the conclusion that a dictator, as a matter of psychological necessity, must never be reminded of his own errors in order to maintain his self-confidence, the ultimate source of his dictatorial force.
I should also like to quote a remark made by Grand Admiral Erich Raeder of the German navy in his book, "My Life." He said:
To have a service. . . dominated by an overburdened politician with no military accomplishments whatsoever, rankled.
I believe this statement describes our feeling toward the present Minister of National Defence. He is prone to making statements which he has to retract later. For example, he made the statement that Admiral Landymore, a gallant officer with a very notable war service, had been disloyal for 18 months before he was fired. If the minister found that this gallant officer was disloyal to Canada before he was fired he was very derelict in his duty in not having him courtmartialled and legally put out of his position rather than just thrown out because he did not agree with the minister's idea of unification of the armed forces. This goes for the 40 other noted, senior officers in the Canadian army, who were fired or forced to resign. The minister should show a great deal more respect for the advice of people who have served and unquestionably have the interests of Canada at heart.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, one of the remarkable things during this debate and during the proceedings of the committee was a constant uttering and re-uttering of hypothetical suggestions for and against the unification of the armed forces.
The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Andras) has indicated that reports in the press were superficial and not serious.
The in-depth study of the report by Mr. Westell in the Globe and Mail reveals contradictory statements in their testimony by witnesses opposed to this legislation. I was most surprised to hear, in the defence committee, an Air Marshal condemn the CF-105 and later admit that he knew nothing about that airplane except what he had heard from others.
I think it is useless to continue arguing back and forth since the interpretation of the government supporters and the opposition is repetitive and time consuming. I think we are in a position to determine here the precise difference in policy between Liberals and Conservatives. Here, in this legislation, is a
National Defence Act Amendment practical reform measure which is fully adapted to change and which would bring about an efficient state of affairs according to our means and our capacities.
On the other hand, we have a negative opposition favouring the status quo and deeply concerned if not buried in the past.
Major General Worthington, in his article published in the Ottawa Journal on April 4, stressed that point most eloquently, as well as the fact that we have to face our responsibilities today and tomorrow.
The reorganization of the Canadian armed forces into a single, flexible and effective service, which is what this bill means, was throughly explained by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) last Monday.
In this connection, it must be borne in mind that members of our armed forces are recruited on a voluntary basis and not, like in many countries, on a compulsory basis.
Air Chief Marshal Miller said in his testimony, that the Canadian armed forces, judging by the country's potential, are the best, as compared to that of any other country. According to international statistics, in Canada, the period of military service is longer than anywhere else.
It is easy to understand, therefore, why the men in our armed forces are better trained than those of other nations.
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) has often mentioned that the morale of the men is not what it should be. However, General Allard has given us the assurance that, at the present time, morale is good, as compared to what it was at certain times in the past.
The hon. member seems to forget the confusion which prevailed in 1963 when he was Minister of National Defence because no decision could be made to equip our weapons with nuclear warheads. This must have irritated servicemen who probably lost any confidence they had in the authorities, at that time.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY. ARMY AND AIF FORCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? If recruiting is as good as he says it is would he explain why our navy is unable to man its ships and why our infantry battalions are seriously under strength?

speechtext: I stated that recruiting has improved since 1966. I stated also that the depletion had been caused by what is called the wartime hump, with practically 24,000 members of the forces leaving because of reaching normal retirement age. I think this is self-explanatory.

speechtext: Would that include General Moncel?

Mr. Chairman, I wish to enter this debate briefly because of my lifelong interest in the military forces of our country and because of my deep interest in the army especially. Before beginning I wish to digress for a moment. I trust, sir, that you will not
