National Defence Act Amendment rule me out of order. I would like to congratulate those members of the government who have been promoted within the last day or two. I congratulate especially the very able former minister without portfolio, now Registrar General, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. I realize only too well that in our system of government the executive has become more powerful over the years and the legislative arm, in which we serve as members, has become of less import. It is vital for governments to have the best men and women that can be found. While I do not wish the ministers a long tenure of office,
I wish them well.
As the Associate Minister of National Defence is in his seat I wish to thank him for the many courtesies he has extended to me. I do not think any member of this house writes more than I do to the associate minister, especially about matters dealing with the immense Canadian forces base at Gagetown. I appreciate the never failing courtesy and help in these matters that have been extended. Though I have not always received the hoped for solution, I know that the minister has always attempted to be helpful, and I thank him for that.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY. ARMY AND AIF FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I said that I would not be too lengthy but I wish to raise several important points. I have tried to approach the unification of our forces with an open mind. It distresses me that the whole development of this measure has proceeded as it has done. I am reasonably certain that many on the government side have grave misgivings about unification. No doubt a few members of my party to some extent agree with unification. Yet it seems to me we have been backed into a position where this has become an almost purely political matter on which the government has taken a fixed position and on which we have adopted a similar posture. I regret this. I have tried to approach this whole question with an open mind, as I said.
Though I believe that integration as originally conceived and implemented was an excellent objective for the minister and the government to have aimed for, from what I have read and heard in the sessions of the defence committee I have attended I am not convinced that we should proceed with unification at this time, certainly not with the haste with which the minister seems to be proceeding.
Among the many representations we have received have been some excellent ones from

DEBATES	April 6, 1967
the Tri-Service Identities Organization, known as TRIO, for short. This body of men gave honourable service in wartime and having returned to civilian life are leaders in their communities across the nation. The position they have taken is not because of political preference. They are deeply concerned about this measure and they have made some excellent suggestions to us, as members of parliament. During my brief address I should like to put on record communication received yesterday from the Tri-Service Identities Organization. I shall comment on each point they make in their letter sent to every member of this house.
Their first point is:
It is noteworthy that not one recently retired senior officer no longer having any attachment to the Department of Defence has supported the program which will be carried forward if Bill C-243 is enacted and everyone of any stature outside the services or government whose military opinion would command respect who has testified before the defence committee has expressed criticism or reservation on the proposed reorganization of the defence establishment.
I attended most of the sessions of the defence committee, either as a member of it when asked to do so by my leader or as an interested observer. The evidence of Air Chief Marshal Miller impressed me more than the evidence of any other officer who appeared there. By this I do not mean to detract from the evidence given by such able men as General Moncel, whom I have known since the war years, Admirals Rayner and Lan-dymore, Air Marshal Annis and General Fleury and others. Their evidence was helpful and it was devastating to the principle of that which this house is asked to enact.
Air Chief Marshal Miller was until a few months ago the senior serving service officer in this country, a distinguished and brilliant officer. I now wish to quote from a Globe and Mail editorial of Wednesday, March 22. I bring this editorial to the attention of the committee because I feel it is so well written, and I should like to place a portion of it on the record. It stresses precisely the point I am raising.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
When Air Chief Marshal Frank Miller retired last July he did so quietly, without any comment about the differences over unification then roiling the armed forces. Until that point, as the first chief of the integrated defence staff, he had been Defence Minister Paul Hellyer's right hand man- how significantly so is indicated by the fact that he had been persuaded to stay three years past the normal retirement age of 55.
The testimony which Air Chief Marshal Miller gave to the Commons defence committee this week
April 6, 1967

is, therefore, of peculiar importance, for it is the testimony of a man who had the regard of the minister, who personified integration, and who studiously observed the duty of an officer not to comment publicly on matters of public policy.
Air Chief Marshal Miller told the committee that unification, while it might well be the end result of integration, would not at present be timely; that more time was needed for the orderly development of the integration process.
One of my hon. friends has put on the record of the house the exact exchange as it took place in the committee, and the testimony given bears out what this editorial has to say.
"I felt that a lot of careful planning was necessary and probably time to educate people was required before the next step of unification." Implementation of the bill could seriously demoralize the forces if it were rushed; the loss of personnel so far had been bad for the forces-"some key men have left."
He said he saw no significant financial or military advantage in unification over integration.
Such testimony from such a man cannot fail to raise serious doubts in any thoughtful member of the committee-or of the public-about the wisdom of Mr. Hellyer's unswerving and headlong rush toward unification. It also raises again the question of what sort of communication has existed in the Defence Department. Air Chief Marshal Miller said he did not think any defence chiefs had advised that unification go ahead, but that the subject had been much discussed. Perhaps discussion and advice are sometimes two names for the same thing-which would suggest that the burden of discussion had been against unification.
I think the point is very clear. None of these knowledgeable senior serving officers, many of whom retired before the final deci-ison to proceed with this measure was taken, support the legislation which is before us.
The second point raised in the letter from the Tri-Service Identities Organization to us is as follows:
Claims that other countries are following the Canadian example have not been substantiated. In fact government intentions as expressed in white papers on defence in the United Kingdom, France and New Zealand show no indication of emulating the Canadian plan which will be carried forward if the bill is enacted. Informed persons in both the U.S.A. and the United Kingdom, as evidenced by recent articles and statements, have indicated concern or disenchantment with the Canadian experiment.
I do not see any particular merit in being the first nation in the world to rush into unification. I think it would be much wiser for us to make haste slowly at this time, to secure one base before moving to another. No other nation in the world today is groping as Canada seems to be doing.

National Defence Act Amendment
The third point raised in this letter is:
The effective strength of the forces is below 104,000 men or 20,000 under the strength at 31st March 1963. The original objective was to reduce the forces by approximately 10,000 men.
I did not disagree with this objective but I feel that the strength of our armed forces has now fallen to a dangerous level. The letter goes on:
Included in this excessive loss are not only many senior officers well in advance of retirement but also many officers in the rank of lieutenant colonel and colonel or equivalent in all three services. In the normal course they would have been available to fill appointments of greater responsibility, yet their retirement must restrict the selection for future leaders. This can have serious repercussions for the future if something is not done to check this exodus.
The fourth point raised in this letter is as follows:
There is evidence of concern over our capability to meet out military commitments as a result of the situation which has developed in the defence department in the last four years.
This, it seems to me, is a vital point for us to consider. It is true we are not one of the great powers of the world though some, including myself, like to think of Canada as being one of the middle powers. Though our population is only 20 million this nation has played a part far more important than might have been expected in the two great wars of the last half century and in the lesser wars which have been fought in Korea and elsewhere. It is significant that in 1914 when our population was only nine or ten million we sent almost 750,000 men and women to fight for democracy. Many of them are still with us including the honourable and gallant member for Winnipeg South Centre, the former defence minister, and others who defended this nation in the great battles such as Pas-schendaele and elsewhere. In the second great war this country put almost a million men and women into the armed forces. Our contribution in northwestern Europe, in Italy and in the Far East, including the tragic episode of Hong Kong, the service of our seamen on Canada's little ships on all the seas of the world, our valiant air force, all made a record far more impressive than might have been expected from a country of our population.
This being the case, our ability to fulfil our military commitments assumes a particular importance. It seems to me that the free nations of the world, and possibly some of those which are not free, have come to expect that when Canada undertakes to do certain things

April 6, 1967
Motions for Papers
it will do them. If the commitments we have undertaken cannot be fulfilled by a unified force we will have been placed in an almost untenable position. Yet this is the opinion, almost without exception, of the expert witnesses who appeared before the committee. I think immediately of General Moncel and of Air Chief Marshal Miller, to mention only two. They have told us that with a unified force it would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to fulfil the commitments we have made to NATO, to NORAD and to the United Nations.

Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock?

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Maiheson (Parliameniary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: GEOGRAPHICAL CO-ORDINATES RESPECTING BASE LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the motion of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) with regard to notes and other communications exchanged between Canada and the United States of America since the enactment by parliament on July 16, 1964, of the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act I think it is useful, if I may, to refer to some of the authorities on this subject.
I should like to refer first to Todd on Parliamentary Government, volume 1, at page 358:
In 1860 a motion in the English House of Commons for the production of a copy of a despatch received from abroad (upon a subject on which negotiations were pending) and before it had been answered, was successfully opposed by the Foreign Secretary (Lord John Russell) on the ground that "such a course would not only be contrary to precedent but contrary to every principle recognized by the constitution:" it "would be like inviting the House to dictate the answer."
Jumping to our own Canadian experience, on February 25, 1929, a member moved for a copy of all letters, cables, correspondence and other documents or agreements entered into by the Canadian government in connection with the Imperial Cable merger of 1928. The postmaster general, Mr. Veniot, asked for the motion to stand as the correspondence was of a private nature between the contracting parties, the different governments of Canada, England, Australia and New Zealand. He pointed out that until permission was received to place that correspondence on the table it could not be tabled.
On January 17, 1939, in the course of debate, not on a motion, the leader of the opposition, Mr. Manion, asked if it would be possible to have published the correspondence relating to the Munich crisis of September, 1938. The prime minister of the day, Mr. April 6. 1967

Mackenzie King, replied that correspondence between governments, particularly where it relates to the possibility of war, is necessarily highly confidential and to make it public would require the consent of the governments concerned. So in that case the motion was denied.
Looking at more recent examples in this chamber I should like to refer to a motion for papers which was brought by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) on the subject of the imposition of United States embargoes. On January 24, 1955, Mr. Diefenbaker asked the government of the day for a copy of all correspondence, letters, telegrams and other documents since May 1, 1954, which had passed between any department of the federal government and the government of the United States regarding the application or imposition by the government of the United States of embargoes, in whole or in part, against importation into the United States of Canadian farm products. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on behalf of the government, indicated that the motion concerned diplomatic correspondence with a former government and dealt with negotiations still in progress. Therefore he maintained that the information was privileged according to the well established practice of the house and that it would not be possible to bring it down at that particular time. The Leader of the Opposition asked that the matter be allowed to stand. The Speaker intervened and added that perhaps in the circumstances it would be better to have the motion dropped. The motion in fact was dropped.
Incidentally, on that same day the Leader of the Opposition also asked Mr. St. Laurent for a copy of all correspondence, letters, telegrams and other documents exchanged since the first day of May, 1954, between any department of government and the governments of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba relative to the South Saskatchewan dam and irrigation project. On that same day Mr. St. Laurent in replying pointed out that since other provinces were concerned this would involve the consent of all these parties.
Moving to the year 1956, we have a motion for the production of papers relating to the Passamaquoddy project and involving an economic feasibility survey. It was motion No. 70 by Mr. Brooks. He asked for everything that had passed between any department or officials of the federal government and the International Joint Commission, the government of the United States of America, and
Motions for Papers
any other government or organization of individuals, relating to a survey or surveys of the economic feasibility of the development of the Passamaquoddy tidal power project. Again the reply was made by the present Prime Minister who referred to the usual rules of privilege regarding international communications. At page 3615 of Hansard for May 7, 1956, he is reported as follows:
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
-in so far as the correspondence with the United States government is concerned, naturally the consent of that government will have to be obtained. In so far as International Joint Commission correspondence is concerned, it has been customary to regard correspondence of this international agency as privileged in this house.
The motion was not debatable and a vote was not taken. Mr. Speaker then said:
This will have to be explored on other occasions. When the hon. member wishes to have his motion debatable he will put it on the order paper without an asterisk. Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion subject to the remarks made by the minister?
By agreement the question was transferred for debate.
Let us then move to 1957 when a new administration was in power headed by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). On December 9 motion No. 45 moved by Mr. Hahn for a copy of the preliminary report entitled proposals for the hydroelectric development of the Columbia river system in Canada was answered on behalf of the government by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) who was at that time the acting minister of northern affairs and natural resources. He said, as reported at page 2083 of Hansard for that date:
Mr. Speaker, I must oppose this motion ... It is a departmental document of a type which is not normally tabled.
He referred to the fact that negotiations with the United States regarding the hydroelectric development of the Columbia river system were taking place and would likely continue for some time, and that it was not in the public interest that these documents be made public during the progress of those negotiations. Mr. Hahn continued to press the matter, at the conclusion of which Mr. Speaker said as reported at page 2084:
That is my recollection, that the document was not quoted except to identify it. This is not a debatable motion. The minister has explained his objection to complying with the order, and all that remains now is to dispose of the motion. Those in favour will please say yea.

speechtext: Nay.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: GEOGRAPHICAL CO-ORDINATES RESPECTING BASE LINES
speechtext:
In my opinion the nays have it. I declare the motion lost.
The precedents to which I am referring relate in every case to correspondence between Canada and some outside agent or country.
Let me refer to Hansard for April 17, 1961, page 3704. On that day Motion No. 100 by Mr. Argue was answered by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), then the minister of veterans affairs. Mr. Argue's motion was:
For a copy of any contract, letter of intent, correspondence, or other documents exchanged between Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited and the United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority since January 1, 1956, in relation to the purchasing of Canadian uranium concentrates by The United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority.
The then minister said in his concluding sentence that the motion could not be accepted. The Speaker then said:
In view of the explanation made by the minister, what is the wish of the mover?
Mr. Argue withdrew the motion. It was dropped, the order was discharged and the motion was withdrawn.
On December 11, 1963 the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) brought a motion for papers in these words:
That an order of the house do issue for a copy of a general assessment of the Battelle institute report to the Alaska international rail and highway commission-
It was motion No. 160. He also requested the recommendations to the United States Congress prepared by the economic division of the department of northern affairs dated May 26, 1961. The present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing) replied in these terms:
I can assure him that If the report which he asked for, dated 1961, were made public It would be accompanied by a series of calculations and recommendations to the government which would demarcate the government's bargaining position in any conclusions or agreements made with the United States government if we arrive at the position where such a mutual undertaking was in prospect.
The hon. member for Yukon responded in the way in which I invite the mover of the motion now before us to respond. The order was discharged and the motion was withdrawn.
There are many other precedents to which I could refer in respect of motions regarding
[Mr. Matheson.i
relations between Canada and other countries. We have built up certain traditions in this house regarding the publication of documents between Canada and provincial governments.
On March 26, 1961 Mr. Jones moved for a copy of letters and other documents between the federal and B.C. governments relating to Indian bands. The response was made by the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickers-gill) who pointed out that while he was prepared to produce the existing correspondence with the government of British Columbia, in respect of correspondence with Indian bands the superintendent of Indian affairs acted as trustee for the Indians in these matters and the correspondence should not be produced unless the Indians agreed. In this case he brought another principle into play. We have heard about the principle in respect of a government or an agency such as atomic energy. We now have the principle in respect of interested parties, in this case the Indians.
On September 3, 1958 Mr. Benidickson moved for a copy of all correspondence since September 1, 1957 between the federal government and the province of Ontario in respect of sharing of costs of the roads to resources program. The motion was responded to by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), then minister of northern affairs. He concluded by saying, as reported at page 4517 of Hansard for that day:
It is impossible to table this correspondence while negotiations are going on because it would embarrass the governments concerned.
On February 2, 1959 the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) moved for a copy of all documents exchanged between the federal government and the government of New Brunswick or the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission concerning the construction of the East Saint John thermal plant. The motion was allowed to stand since negotiations between the governments were still in progress and it would have been improper to produce the papers at that time.
There is a great deal of relevance to some of the precedents I have just cited, particularly when we consider that the motion of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is for a copy of notes and other communications exchanged between Canada and the United States since July 16, 1964 in respect of lists of geographical co-ordinates or points from which base lines may be determined in accordance with the provisions of the act.
April 6, 1967

On January 18, 1961, the hon. member tor Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), a member of the party to which the hon. member for Co-mox-Alberni belongs, moved for a copy of all correspondence and documents exchanged between the department of northern affairs and national resources and the B.C. government regarding the development of hydro resources on the Columbia River. The minister speaking for the government at that time was the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), who opposed production until negotiations with the United States were over and the agreement ratified. The motion was withdrawn.
On April 17, 1961, Mr. Argue moved for a copy of any contract or other documents-I will not go into the details-exchanged between Eldorado Mining and Refining Ltd. and the United Kingdom atomic energy authority since January 1, 1956. As I mentioned before, the then minister of veterans affairs, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), felt that they could not be produced and in fact they were not produced.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
While wishing to be co-operative, it is clear that there has been established in this house an important principle in this regard. To depart from this principle would occasion embarrassment to a government faithfully carrying out confidential negotiations with another country, a province or agency. For the foregoing reasons, Mr. Speaker, I very much regret that the government does not find it possible to accede to the hon. member's request.

speechtext:
I certainly agree with you, sir. The N.D.P. and those of us on this side of the house are interested in the House of Commons and we should return to the matter under discussion. I wish to review briefly what brought about the discussion on the production of papers in connection with the 12-mile fishing limit. Some changes are taking place in the fisheries of the world which need to be emphasized from time to time because they affect the livelihood of many Canadians. This question is important to our trade abroad. It is important to the future growth and development of Canadian trade and to the employment of people on both our coasts. Therefore I think it important to review some of these points for a moment or two.
When the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) spoke on February 9 last on this motion the argument he put forward was that the matter before the house was in reality a motion for the production of papers. He based his argument on that point. However, I want to go behind the motion to what gives rise to it. A matter of very grave interest gave rise to the motion of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett). It was my privilege last year, at the outset of this session when the estimates were brought down, to have the opportunity to chair the fisheries committee in its examination of the estimates. It was an exercise which I enjoyed

April 6, 1967
Motions for Papers
very much and from which I hope I have profited.
I entered the committee room with other hon. members knowing virtually nothing about Canada's fisheries and found myself the chairman of a group who were very expert in this field. There were hon. members from both sides of the house, representing coastal constituencies and constituencies with inland fisheries, who had long been accustomed to looking after the needs of fishermen and thinking in terms of the Canadian fisheries economy. It was a pleasure to me to have the opportunity of associating with them and to explore with the Department of Fisheries, the Fisheries Research Board and the minister the grave problems affecting not only the Canadian fisheries industry but the world food and world population situation. This makes our Canadian fisheries so important and it makes our discussion of the 12-mile limit very pertinent.
After its examination of the estimates the committee made four recommendations to the minister. We recommended that the efforts and research of the department be strengthened in these areas: first of all, coastal pollution and pollution of our inland waters; second, increased research and the development in particular of methods which would bring to commercial feasibility the artificial production and spawning of lobster on the east coast and salmon on the west coast. Our third recommendation concerned the policing of some of our subsidized fisheries programs and, fourth, we dealt with the incursion of foreign fishing fleets into Canadian waters, which is the subject at hand and about which we were considerably worried at that time.
The world situation in respect of food needs no elucidation in this house other than to say that the world population is exploding at an unprecedented rate and our capability of finding food for the population of the world is not meeting that expansion. Hence, people in countries are going to sea as they have never gone to sea before in an effort to find the food and the proteins necessary to feed their vastly expanding populations. This has given rise to a number of changes in the fishing industry. First of all, the United States itself, although a wealthy nation and capable of taking care of the food needs of its own people, has become an importer of fish and fish products to an increasing extent. This has provided for Canada an increasing U.S. market.

[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
It is of particular interest that the expansion of the market in the U.S. has been characterized by a great expansion on the west coast, particularly in the state of California where much of the increase in the west coast fishery market is now being found. It is a fact that European fishing fleets, long accustomed to fishing off the Grand Banks and in the waters of the Canadian east coast, now find they are bringing an increasing amount of their catch back to the European market and less to the U.S. market which they have long served. So the European market is making increasing demands upon that particular fishery. These demands have extended to the extent that the fisheries of the east coast are beginning to reach a balance of production, and it will not be too long before the world's greatest ground fisheries will be in danger of over-fishing and measures of conservation will have to be applied.
On the west coast we are experiencing for the first time the sight of foreign vessels in considerable numbers fishing off that coast with massive fishing equipment the like of which the Canadians and Americans accustomed to fishing that coast have never seen. I speak particularly of the huge Russian fishing fleets which have moved in around the entrances to the Canadian coast to the south and north of the Queen Charlotte islands, and also of the Russian fisheries fishing off the Aleutians and down the coast of Alaska, in addition to the increase in the Japanese fisheries fishing off that coast. This has come about simply because of the need to find protein for the increasing population of those countries. It has come about also as a part of the increasing technology of those countries and their capability of engaging in a major fishery based on huge equipment and done upon a very scientific basis.
It is this innovation on the west coast, at a time when our own ground fishery is increasing, that frightens the people of that area in respect of their fisheries, and of the future of their fisheries, if methods cannot be found and agreements cannot be reached to protect these great inland fisheries from being fished out by foreign fleets hungry for proteins for their starving and undernourished peoples.
We have other reasons for being interested in the growth of the ground fisheries, the protection of which is associated with the establishment of a 12-mile limit. We are accustomed on the west coast to the salmon
April 6, 1967

fishery which is fished only when the runs are on, and this comes over a very short period of time. Then the canneries operate for a very short period of time, and when that is finished the man who is engaged, either in fishing salmon at sea or in the cannery, finds his work done. If it were not for other kinds of fish and other methods of fishing on the west coast the fishing industry there would be a very ephemeral and seasonal occupation indeed. But it has been because of the development of the ground fishery that the fishing season and the use of vessels and canneries have been spread out to occupy a much longer period during the year and to make of the fisheries on the west coast a much more stable industry.
This has meant that the fishing industry has had to get into business with much heavier equipment, with boats 60, 70 and 80 feet in length, vessels costing upward of $100,000, $200,000 and $300,000, and equipment and gear which is very expensive to operate and which must be amortized over a considerable period of time, and as the result of a very stable fishery. It has also meant that the old fashioned fishery, which was an old wooden shed with very little equipment in it, has been modernized into the most modern plants that you will see in Canada involved in the packaging and processing of food. It has meant that these plants are engaged in much more work in the course of a year, to process the fish brought in by trawlers which are now working on the ground fisheries off the coast of northern British Columbia and in the Pacific coastal waters.
There is a further development which is of interest to us as Canadians. One plant on the west coast has now a subsidiary operating in California. This subsidiary is receiving frozen fish blocks which are used for cutting up into fish sticks and portions, which it is packaging and selling in the U.S. market. So we are not only expanding a Canadian industry but we are engaging in the development of a foreign trade and establishing plants in the United States. I think the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) would be delighted if he could hear this explanation of the very reverse of what he considers to be American imperialism in Canadian industry. This is more a case of Canadian imperialism in the United States, and it is very desirable from the standpoint of the west coast industry.
All this means that the fishery on the west coast, which once provided only a portion of the livelihood of people, has now become a
Motions for Papers
very stable industry, not only at sea but on land and in the export trade, one that is capable of employing an increasing number of people and engaging a larger segment of the economy. Therefore it is essential, and becomes increasingly so, that this kind of fishery be well protected. There are several ways in which this can be achieved. One way of course is in the development of treaties and arrangements with regard to conservation between the United States and ourselves, and any others who may fish in these waters both on the west and the east coast, to see that we do not fish out these fisheries; because if we cannot conserve them, not only will they be of no good to us but they will be of no good to the rest of the world which relies on these fisheries for the food they so badly need.
The second point I want to drive home is that these fisheries are an off-shore resource of the Canadian people, and to whatever extent possible we as a nation should do what is in our power to protect this resource for our own people as a source of employment for them, and as a source of the future development of our own markets abroad.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
We do not object, as Canadians, to the historic fisheries that have been developed in the waters off our shores over periods of hundreds of years, since the discovery of this continent. However, I believe there must be a recognition of the fact that we have some rights in these waters, and in the fisheries which we have taken the trouble to conserve and for which we have developed markets. It is important that we be aggressive as Canadian people in establishing the 12-mile limit and in protecting the bays of our offshore waters which are necessary to the conservation of these fisheries.
I cannot therefore be too forceful in urging upon the government and upon the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud), who I understand at this moment is in Russia discussing this question, amongst others, with his counterpart in the Russian government, the need to reach an agreement with the operators of the world's major fisheries on behalf of the Canadian people. In the last little while the United States has been successful in negotiating a 12-mile limit for Alaskan waters. They have had to make some concessions in order to achieve this. They have had to give the Russians a concession which enables them to come into Alaskan ports for food, for ship repairs and the like.

April 6, 1967
Motions for Papers
Of course, this kind of concession enables the Russian fleet to maintain itself offshore and engage in extensive fishing beyond the 12-mile limit for a longer period of time. This represents a considerable concession the United States had to make in order to establish this limit. We, to date, have not been too badly put upon by the massive fleets which the Russians are able to bring to bear on these fisheries. We have had a taste of this on the west coast, so that we know the initial, exploratory work in our ground fishery has been done by these foreign fleets. A serious problem is shaping up for us in the future, if we do not rest on top of it.
In closing, therefore, I want to say that I am glad to see this motion on the order paper because of the opportunity it provides to discuss this serious matter and emphasize to the government of the day, which I am proud to support, that this is a serious matter for those of us who live on the coast. We hope that the efforts of the minister, when he is in Russia, will be fruitful and that he will continue to impress upon the Russians, as well as our United States neighbours, who are tough customers to deal with on the subject of fishing in Canadian waters, that these Canadian resources should be used for the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this motion because of the vital importance of the subject to fishermen and because of my particular interest both in the geographical co-ordinates and the 12-mile limit. The question, I believe, is whether it is desirable

to make public the notes and communications requested, and also if it is possible or proper, in light of the rules governing diplomatic correspondence, to produce these documents and letters exchanged between one government and another while negotiations are still continuing.
I should like in a moment to come back to a discussion of whether or not it is proper, and I do not believe it is. First of all, I should like to deal with the question of whether it is desirable to produce these papers. It would seem, Mr. Speaker, that by producing them at this time there would be an adverse effect on the negotiations taking place with other nations with regard to the establishment of the 12-mile limit. The 12-mile limit and the establishment of the co-ordinates are of vital importance. One hears now of cases of foreign draggers coming into our inshore waters and ruining the gear of our shore fishermen. This results of course in damage to the gear and a loss of catch. The continued activities of these draggers is resulting in a reduction in the amount of fish being taken by the shore fishermen, so there is an adverse effect on their living. The continued expansion of these foreign fleets and the methods they use for taking the fish have resulted in a reduction in the catch of our Canadian draggers who are operating farther out. We must look also at the fact that the world relies on the sea for food. We must therefore maintain the fish we have in the ocean, to maintain the world food supply. The control we would have through the establishment of these limits as a result of negotiations with other countries would be of utmost importance, both in establishing where these operations should take place, and in establishing the type of fish that should be taken.
We hear of cases where certain of these draggers using new systems are taking fish of all types, keeping the type they want and throwing the others overboard. This means that there are dead fish floating around which could have been used. Negotiations between the various countries would assist in both controlling the fishery and in ensuring that it will continue.
This excessive dragging in certain inshore areas has resulted in a reduction in the catch of the shore fishermen. This reduction has occurred for two reasons. In the first place, these large draggers from other countries are taking an excessive amount of fish, with the consequent reduction in catch for our fishermen. There has been a reduction in catch also as a result of the fact they have disturbed the
April 6, 1987

area in which spawning takes place. The fact these operations have moved inshore has reduced the amount of fish in these areas and has forced our shore fishermen to move farther out. They have been forced to use larger boats and heavier gear. At the same time, the trawlers move through these areas and cause damage to the gear, as I mentioned before, and this has a serious effect.
The desire to establish a limit is not new, but it is of vital importance that we should have it. It is also important that we should discuss with other countries the appropriate limit we should have, so that it can be recognized by those countries which are fishing near our shores.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
Some of the limits that have been set were set early in the 1900's. Norway declared her limit of four miles in 1906. In 1907 Argentina declared a limit of 12 miles; in 1909 Spain declared a limit of 6 miles; in 1912 Italy declared a limit of 7 miles; and in 1914 Greece declared a limit of 6 miles. Colombia declared a limit of 12 miles, Ecuador 15 miles, Korea 50 to 60 miles, the Dominican Republic 12 miles, El Salvador 200 miles, Cambodia 12 miles, India 100 miles and Ceylon 100 miles. These limits have already been declared by these countries.
However, I think we all realize that declaring a limit without the agreement of other countries who might want to fish off shore is not satisfactory. It would take a tremendous number of patrol boats to patrol a limit of, as is the case with some countries, 100 or 200 miles, and in view of this ineffective patrolling the limit could not be enforced.
Talking of our present limits and regulations, by agreement and by regulation the Department of Fisheries is doing an excellent job of patrolling both with the use of patrol boats and planes. I feel that this effort on their part would be improved if the limit were increased, and we had the agreement of other nations to such extension.
The effect of a limit on our fishery shows the importance of any bill to make this provision. It must be established here whether this production of papers would serve the purpose of protecting our fishermen and our fishery. It appears to me that the production of these documents would have an adverse effect upon the implementation of the base lines and of a 12-mile limit. It is necessary to make this provision under international law, and we must make sure that other countries obey such a limit.
Motions for Papers
In 1947 the United Nations set up the international law commission. Ten years later that commission, after a very exhaustive study of every aspect, presented a report covering this whole topic. In 1957 the United Nations called for a conference to be held in Geneva in 1958, and the conference was held in February through to April of that year, 86 nations attending. Progress was made. They did not make as much progress on this limit as we would have wished, but effective discussions were held. These discussions between the nations are what will make effective the provision of a 12-mile limit and the setting of base line co-ordinates.
If we do something at this point which will disrupt the negotiations we are having with the United States and other nations, the effect would be to set back the discussions we have already had and the possibility of bringing in the 12-mile limit within a short period of time. This would result in a further spate of discussions, which would set off to a later date still the setting of a limit.
These limits are of vital importance to the continuation of the fishery both on the west coast and on the east coast, where larger ships of other nations are moving in. Russian fleets have lately started to move in. The Soviet Union has developed even larger and more modern vessels, and their techniques are such that they are able to net a larger amount of fish than some of our traditional fishing neighbours who come from long distances across the sea. The Portuguese have been fishing off our east coast for some 500 years; and some of our American neighbours to the south have been coming into what are Canadian waters and taking what are the resources of Canada for many years.
When the limit is brought in we will have to recognize, at least for a limited time, some of the traditional rights of these countries. However, it is desirable-indeed, it is a requirement-that we gradually withdraw some of these rights, particularly in the case of vessels which are coming closer in to the shore.
The fishery on the east coast has been carried on almost since the time the continent was discovered. When the first settlers located along the coast of Newfoundland in the early 1500's they started to fish. Other crews came out from Europe to fish, and then returned at the end of the fishing season.
From that date, Mr. Speaker, the fishing industry has grown each year, although we have had the occasional bad year. It is now

April 6, 1967
Business of the House
undergoing, especially on the east coast, a tremendous change in that new methods are being adopted in an effort to modernize the industry and assist the fishermen to obtain larger catches of fish as well as to market better products. At the same time the value of these efforts is being lessened by the fact that foreign draggers are operating offshore and closer inshore than they should, which both reduces the amount of fish available to be fished and hurts the grounds where the fish breed and spawn.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we must move as quickly as possible to bring in the 12-mile limit and control the method of fishing this area. If we were to produce these papers and disrupt the present negotiations, all progress would be hindered and virtually stopped. So I suggest that the papers requested should not be produced, because of the adverse effect this would have on the industry.
The fishing industry is divided into many parts-the shore fishery, the fishery from longliners and the fishery by trawler. The amount of fish taken from the shore has been increasing as the fishermen have improved their methods. Other methods of fishing have also improved. The amount of fish that the trawlers and larger ships, particularly the ships of other nations, are able to take has increased to a far greater extent and, as I have already mentioned, an adverse effect on our fishery.
In order to protect our fishermen, then, I suggest that we should not produce these papers at this time.

As a basis for my remarks on this subject I was using a letter received from the Tri-Service Identities Organization by all members of parliament a few days ago. The point in the letter to which I was addressing my remarks was the fourth, which reads as follows:
There is evidence of concern over our capability to meet our military commitments as a result of the situation which has developed in the Defence Department in the last four years.
When the able and distinguished former senior officers were before us, I took occasion, as did many other members of the committee, to ask General Foulkes, General Moncel and others whether they believed that if the forces of this country were unified we could discharge the commitments we have made to NATO, to NORAD and to the United Nations. Every one of these military leaders stressed the point that they did not believe we could
National Defence Act Amendment fulfil our present obligations under unification. I will admit that the Minister of National Defence did not agree with this, and he said so on several occasions, once in answer to a question I put to him. However, the evidence is there, for the record, in the committee reports. The able officers who gave evidence before the committee did not agree with the minister on that point.
Next I should like to place on record the fifth and sixth paragraphs of this letter, which are related.
(5)	Expenditures on equipment for the five years ending the 31st March, 1968 will not match the spending for the five years ending the 31st March, 1963 despite claims that the reorganization is to make more money available for equipment.
(6)	It is admitted that the steps in the reorganization which will be possible under Bill C-243 will not lead to savings of any account. Thus, if any savings are possible, it will be as a result of those steps taken since 1964 under the authority of Bill C-90. Bill C-243 having been categorized as permissive, the wisdom of proceeding at this time would seem to be questionable if economies are not to be effected and in face of the widespread criticism which the department's program is encountering.
One of the arguments in favour of unification which appealed to a great many people in this country is that a considerable proportion of our military budget could be saved each year if unification were carried out. This would be a valid argument, if it were true. But it would appear from the evidence placed before the committee which examined this bill that such is not the case. As this letter points out, there will not be as much money available for equipment in the next five years as there was in the past, and the economies which have been effected up to this stage have resulted from integration, not from unification. Again I would suggest that there is very little opposition either in this house, in the country as a whole or in the armed forces themselves to the principle of integration: It is unification which is disturbing all of us.
The seventh paragraph is one in which I am deeply interested and reads as follows:
It has been admitted that morale should be improved. Many service personnel are deeply disturbed by the uncertainty which now exists for a service career and are unwilling to accept the reorganization as they now see it. Nothing should be done to aggravate this situation.
In my discussions with servicemen as I travel back and forth across the eastern part of this country I have found that a great many are deeply disturbed about what is happening, although there are, of course, some who are not giving the matter much thought.
April 6, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment Recently I was talking to a young helicopter pilot who was travelling from Halifax to Toronto. His feeling was that a great many key personnel were simply waiting to see What would happen, and that if this bill were to become law there could very well be a considerable exodus of key personnel from the armed forces. This would be tragic, especially when we have lost so many capable men already.
Paragraphs eight and nine of the letter read as follows:
(8)	It seems remarkable that the critics of the reorganization have been variously categorized as emotional, unprogressive, unreasonable, disloyal, obstructionist, destructive, politically motivated or without responsibility. Do none of the extensive body of Canadians who hold opinions contrary to those of the minister of defence do so by reason of knowledge, capability, experience, conviction, concern or sincerity? Surely the calibre of some of the witnesses who have appeared before the defence committee dictates a high degree of credibility for their views and in no way justifies any discounting of their evidence and opinions.
(9)	Overwhelming support for the reorganization program does not exist amongst Canadians generally. Thus the latest Gallup poll showed less than 50 per cent of Canadians support it. Observing that this poll was taken before the defence committee started its hearings, and before so much cogent evidence was presented by so many knowledgeable persons against the plans and policies as presently disclosed, would certainly permit the conclusion that even fewer Canadians support the program now than six weeks ago.
That is indeed an interesting observation. Finally:
(10)	The military merit of the proposed reorganization has not been established in the light of our declared military commitments at least to the satisfaction of experienced ex-senior officers who appeared before the committee.
In summary I submit that no legislation has been presented to you during the long session now drawing to a close which has less justification or foundation for enactment than Bill C-243 as it is now written. While it is possible that amendments may be made to make the bill acceptable, these would have to go to the root of the legislation, namely section 2, and provide for the continuance of the navy, army and air force, the identities of which will be abolished under the present proposals. As this would in effect nullify much of what is now proposed, on balance the prudent and proper course would be to shelve the proposed bill and thereby the program which will be made possible thereunder pending further examination of all aspects of our defence.
I dealt with this aspect earlier in my address.

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say again that I think a great many officers and men in the services believe integration is

a good thing. It has had beneficial results, but two or three years are required for it to shake down before it will have its full effect. Undoubtedly it will be beneficial. It has proven to be beneficial up to this point, but I believe, as I feel a great many Canadians do, that we should now proceed with caution. This particular bill at this time should stand, let us say, six months or a year, at which time it might be raised again when the feelings of opposition perhaps have lessened, when worries have been quietened, and when there is more evidence to show that unification is a step which we should take in respect of the whole organization of the armed forces of this country.

Mr. Chairman, it was my understanding that this debate, if debate it is, was supposed to be a discussion of the bringing up to date of Canada's armed forces in the world which we face in the late 1960's and early 1970's. We are supposed to be debating a program to bring Canada's armed forces into line so that they will be able to deal with the new technology with which our forces are equipped, and with which they are to be equipped. This means, Mr. Chairman, that when we are debating this subject we should be debating the form we want the army, the air and naval forces to take, and what we want them to do. It means that our judgment must be on the basis of efficiency and effectiveness, because armed forces are expensive.
Unification, as I understand it, implies the merging of administrative and support functions, command functions, command responsibility, personnel management, supply services, pay services, recruitment and training. To me it means taking a three dimensional look at our armed forces, and the world in which we must use them. The last time I participated in this debate on this subject I said that to me defence is only a function of foreign policy, and therefore we should take a look at our foreign policy to see what policies we intend to follow in order to determine what kind of force we require to fulfil those policies.
Yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs gave us a most interesting tour of the world, as it appears to him. He underlined the assumptions and attitudes the Canadian government is taking in determining the function that the armed forces would perform as a result of this particular bill. In going over his speech, I find that he seemed to make three points. First, he said we were in NORAD to defend North America, because
April 6, 1967

this is the collective way to do it, and that the United States is a pillar upon which all western security has been based since the second world war. Furthermore he intimated that one of the reasons France was withdrawing from the NATO alliance was that France was not willing to assume that the United States would stand up to protect her any longer.
The second point he made is that NATO now is basically a political alliance, whereas in its beginning it had been basically a military alliance designed to protect both Europe and North America from sudden attack from Russia. Things are changing. The NATO alliance itself now is in danger of breaking up, since the withdrawal of France and the subsequent moving of NATO headquarters to Brussels. The minister pointed out that it is necessary for all countries concerned with NATO to re-examine their position to see whether it is necessary to maintain the alliance under the present circumstances.
The third function which Canada has performed in a military way is that of participation in United Nations peace keeping operations in Cyprus and on the Israel-U.A.R. border. In addition it has provided observers on the frontiers of Israel, Syria, Jordan, Lebanon and Kashmir. Canada also participates in the International Supervisory Commission in Indo China, although this function of course does not come under the United Nations jurisdiction.
This is the basis for our foreign policy as the minister outlined it. It indicates a shifting role for Canada in its foreign affairs and in the role our military forces should play in order to take their full part. In other words, we seem to be moving away from what could be described as a static position or a holding operation to a position where our forces would be mobile and capable of moving quickly to trouble spots wherever they may be, and wherever our forces may be required.
I should like to remind hon. gentlemen that since the second world war we have had some 40 odd bushfires, small wars, which have broken out. It is this type of operation which I believe will require the participation of the smaller nations, such as Canada, which do not have any great interest in founding an empire, if you like, or in furthering their own national goals. We are able to go in as detached observers, and we have had fairly good results in this field.
National Defence Act Amendment
There have been a number of arguments raised against unification. I think that basically they resolve into two arguments of substance. The first and most difficult to attack is the argument that we are going too far too fast. It is difficult for those of us in the House of Commons who are not experts in these fields to determine whether or not we indeed are going too far too fast. However, whether we should use this argument as a means to impede progress is another matter. My own feeling is that the argument, that we are going too far too fast, is the argument used by Conservatives when they wish to stop movements which are progressive in nature. In other words, this is the natural Conservative reaction to a progressive proposal. I would suggest to those newspaper reporters and editors who have said that there is no Conservative party in Canada that the defence debate we are having here is a perfect example of this, in the way they are putting forward the argument "too far too fast".

Mr. Chairman, although I have not had the privilege of being a member of the committee dealing with this important subject I must confess at the outset that this is the third time I have participated in the debate. First I participated at the resolution stage. I did so again at second reading, and I am doing so now as we proceed toward third reading. I do so because I am becoming increasingly amazed at the government's tactics as they proceed from stage to stage in dealing with this particular piece of legislation. There is an old saying that what matters is not what you do but the way in which you do it.
As I have followed the deliberations in the committee and the discussions during the current third reading stage I have been amazed at the government's, and in particular the minister's, persistence in trying to bulldoze the legislation before us through the house, regardless of the evidence that was produced in the recent deliberations of the committee and regardless of the very sound arguments that have been propounded in the course of the debate at the present time, arguments which are largely gleaned from the voluminous committee reports which prove beyond the shadow of a doubt that there is a crediti-bility gap in what the minister has been presenting with reference to the present discussion.
Not so long ago the minister was being hailed across the nation as a miracle worker in reorganizing Canada's armed forces. The press in general, with minor exceptions, was loud in its praise of the manner in which the
April 6, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment new minister was proceeding to accelerate the process of integration which has been going on in Canada for the past ten years. I know the suggestion has been put forward in this debate that this is an idea which has emerged from the new Liberal government and from the minister himself, but anyone who has been in touch with military affairs not only in this country but in other nations as well knows that every modern nation has been endeavouring to reorganize its armed forces on the basis of the integration principle, that is integration at the command level.
Having proceeded successfully thus far I am amazed to find the minister, seemingly supported at this stage by his very capable public relations service which up until recent times has been able to steer the press in the right direction, destroying his reputation, and permitting his reputation to be tarnished by a bullheaded approach to a policy which can only result in the destruction of our defence potential in carrying out our obligations and our various international commitments. This is an argument put forward not only by a stubborn opposition; it is an argument which has been put forward by men who were in key positions less than a year ago and who had the responsibility of carrying out the integration program.
The present government's stance is also being criticized to an increasing extent by the members of the fourth estate. One of the newspapers which has been most critical is one which has been known as the voice of Liberalism on the prairies, namely the Winnipeg Free Press. Since this debate started they have once again been thundering editorially against the nihilistic, destructive program of the government with reference to its decision to go the ultimate degree in destroying Canada's defence potential. Indeed the latest editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press, which appeared on April 4, is headed "Destroying Defence". I should like to read one pertinent paragraph which sums up in the proverbial nutshell the case we have been trying to make. Of course I take this on my own responsibility. It reads as follows:
This revolutionary gamble and experiment is being foisted on Canada in face of the strongest possible protest by nearly every experienced admiral, general and air marshal in the country. If this step could simply be classed as a further blunder by an accident-prone government, and could be corrected when its faults became clearly apparent, the country could perhaps afford to go along for the ride. When it is realized, however, that Mr. Hellyer is playing with an annual investment of some $1.6 billion which vitally concerns

the defence structure of the nation and involves our international obligations, the magnitude of this error becomes obvious.
That is the voice of Liberalism in midwestern Canada, the Winnipeg Free Press.

There is a sense of shock, too, that the government, in our centennial year, should be proceeding with a policy that is so destructive of our traditions. We had hoped that this session would have been concluded before Easter, and that we could have proceeded with a new session known as the centennial session, when we could have taken under consideration more positive and beneficial programs for this nation. Instead, the decision has been made, notwithstanding everything that has been said by the opposition, by the press and by military authorities, to press on regardless of this tradition destroying process.
It is little wonder that one of the distinguished members of the press gallery who has just completed a centennial survey of the nation endeavouring to get the pulse by visiting every capital, by talking to each of our provincial premiers-I refer to Mr. Peter Newman-summed up his series by saying he found that Canada was suffering from neuroses. How could it be otherwise, when you have a government which deliberately creates a situation of division that seems to be based on the old Pavlovian psychological technique of blowing hot and cold to such an extent that not only is the government confused but they have confused the whole nation. The centennial commissioner, John Fisher-I have heard him on this theme many times-constantly urges Canadians to get off the psychiatrist's couch, to move forward on positive lines, to think in terms of things that hold us together, to emphasize those things which unite us rather than those things which divide us.
The approach of the government toward the bill now before us almost reflects the spirit of anarchy that is abroad in the world today. The tendency to describe members of the opposition as ignoramuses, because they did not agree with his viewpoint, was also subdued somewhat. I think perhaps this was more the result of the recent press criticism that has arisen rather than any criticism that has come from this highest court of public opinion. The press has been criticial of the minister's unbending,

Here is a group in the house that is taking its position in opposition, in this debate, on the basis of a situation which absolutely refutes the stand that has been taken by the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
To conclude, Mr. Chairman, I say that the important criterion in our armed forces, if they are to maintain the standard of excellence achieved up to the present point, is to maintain unity of purpose and strong, positive motivation. This can be done only by keeping alive that esprit de corps which made it possible for Canadians to stand at Vimy Ridge. It

National Defence Act Amendment has been said several times that what happened there laid the foundations for our nationhood, as we understand it, and we commemorate that occasion in this our centennial year.

[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
No doubt if one examines the expenditures of the Department of National Defence for the fiscal year 1961-62, comparing them with the fiscal year 1967-68, he could certainly conclude that defence today is costing Canada more than it cost in 1961-62. Such a statement can only be made if certain relevant factors are ignored, for example the fact that dollars do not remain constant over a six-year period. Such a statement can only be made if we forget or ignore the fact that the cost of sophisticated military equipment has increased tremendously over the past five years; it can only be made if we turn a blind eye to the percentage of the total budget

which is devoted to defence, or if we ignore the fact that a new system of reflecting increased pension costs has been included in the defence budget. Such a statement can only be made if one neglects to consider the increases in civilian and military salaries over the past six years. Those who ignore these factors are evading the truth and creating a false impression with regard to savings and expenditures.
I should like to emphasize that in the period 1964-65 through to 1966-67 considerable savings were in fact achieved even though the factors which I have just mentioned are ignored. subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext: That is an admission.

The Dominion Bureau of Statistics has reported that the price index in connection with expenditures in the government sector of the economy rose from 110.3 in 1961 to an estimated 135.4 in 1966-the 1966 figure is based on a nine months period and contains an element of projection. The base year for these figures is 1957, with the index at 100. Now the defence budget for 1967-68, namely $1,688 million, would amount to only $1,375 million in terms of 1961-62 dollars, which is some $251 million less than the actual expenditure in 1961-62. On the other hand, in terms of 1966 dollars the defence expenditure for 1961-62, namely $1,626,104,000, would amount to more than $2 billion.
Perhaps some hon. gentlemen opposite- and this is obviously the case-do not appreciate the relevance of the comparison. But this is not a hypothetical or academic argument. Any statement to the effect that more money or less is being spent today than was spent in some previous year can only be made on a fair basis of comparison, and purchasing power as reflected in the price index is the only reasonable basis for such comparison.
Again it is hardly reasonable to suggest that the government is spending more on defence today than it did previously, when the percentage of the total government budget devoted to the Department of National Defence has declined considerably in the past four years. In 1963-64 the percentage allotted to defence amounted to 24.5; today, the departmental budget amounts to about 14 per cent. Ten years ago, 6 per cent of Canada's gross national product was allocated for defence. Today the percentage is 2.7.

National Defence Act Amendment entire reorganization program. I do not think, however, if one views the developments in the light of all the facts rather than by taking a selection of the facts that the statement I just have made can be contested.
The other point with which I should like to deal relates to the contribution made by the hon. member for Greenwood yesterday or the day before, and by his alter ego in the defence strategy field, Mr. Gellner. The hon. member for Greenwood was very critical of the role that the Canadian Armed Forces are required to play in NATO. Arguing largely with the views expressed by Mr. Gellner, the hon. member for Greenwood questioned the acceptability or the contemporary quality of the modern NATO strategy both in terms of the type of war we might expect in Europe, or lack of war, and the strategy of deterrence. He questioned the role of the CF-104 in Europe and also I believe the role of the brigade group.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Much of the argument presented by the hon. member for Greenwood makes some sense. I for one would be extremely worried as a member on the back benches of this government if I did not feel confident that our role in NATO is indeed under constant review. The suggestion by the hon. member
April 6. 1967

National Defence Act Amendment for Greenwood, however, was that regardless of the position of the alliance and regardless of the position of our allies, what we should do is take arbitrary and unilateral action on our own part to decide ourselves what our role in Europe should be and then, I suppose, present it to our allies as a fait accompli.
It would seem to me that one of the fundamental conditions of a partnership in any form of alliance is that questions involving the long term strategy and the role of individual members of that alliance should not be questions which are decided by individual members unilaterally or arbitrarily. If alliances are to have any meaning, such subjects as these must be negotiated collectively. It may make for good rhetoric, it may be a popular position to take, and it may have all the attributes of a courageous, independent stand to say that we should develop an individual position here-a unique position, a Canadian position-and that our allies should adapt themselves to our concept of what our role will be, but this is the position which the leader of the French republic has taken and we know what the result has been. subtopic: SITTING RESUMED

There may be a question of semantics involved here, because in his concluding remarks at page 14449 of Hansard the hon. member for Greenwood made this point:
In conclusion I would say to the minister that even at this late date it is time to use some imagination; it is time to use something in the nature of a stirring appeal to the people of Canada. Only a truly Canadian defence policy can obtain the support for which the minister asks in relation to his plans for unification.
Although that statement is not directly relevant, it is relevant in part. My interpretation of the remarks of the hon. member for Greenwood is that the Canadian position


should be-as it actually is-determined by ourselves, but that his approach seems to have the overtures of a rather self-centred or unilateral position. I do not know whether the hon. member for Greenwood would support a position of withdrawal, assuming he could not persuade our allies. If I have mistated the position of the hon. member for Greenwood, I submit that at least for my benefit he should clarify his position, although it may be presumptuous of me to say this.
This brings me to the final point I should like to make in respect of the position taken by the hon. member for Greenwood and I can only assume also by the group of which he is a member. It relates to this line which appears at page 14449 of Hansard:
Only a truly Canadian defence policy can obtain the support for which the minister asks in relation to his plans for unification.
My interpretation of that is that the position of the hon. member for Greenwood is that unless the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State for External Affairs are prepared to accede to the position-which I think is an untenable position and one which is inconsistent with the position of a member of the alliance-which we are presently discussing, his party probably will not lend their support to Bill C-243. In other words, they are not refuting the principle of unification. They seem to be in accord with it; but there appears to be an element of argument they are introducing in which there seems to be a suggestion that they might withdraw their support for the bill if the terms suggested by the hon. member for Greenwood in respect of the position Canada should take are not accepted.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit another question. Is he in fact accusing us of subterfuge because we introduced the question of the relationship of the role our forces are to play in NATO to the issue of unification? Does he not also think that perhaps some of the senior officials in the Canadian armed forces are guilty of the same thing, because more than one has said that unification of our armed forces and the maintenance of our present role in NATO would make it rather more difficult. This is the position that my colleague has been taking as well.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
No. The position of most of the witnesses who appeared before the committee on national defence related directly to the bill itself. I say that the hon. member for
April 6, 1967

Greenwood has taken the position that in effect we do not have a defence policy, and that we are not presenting a distinctly Canadian position. What the hon. member is saying is that unless we adopt the position he is prepared to support-and this position has been disputed by myself and others, namely that we take a different approach to an alliance by adopting a heavy-handed attitude and negotiate an alliance which embraces our strategic concepts-he is not in agreement. Let me state that we are at this time carrying out negotiations. I do not think the hon. member for Greenwood can reasonably suggest that this government is not negotiating new roles for NATO and possible new roles for Canada on a continuing basis. To introduce this element of argument, when in fact something in this regard is being done, as a condition for support for this bill is unreasonable. Does the hon. member not think that Canada should establish its own defence and foreign policies and institute them on a unilateral basis or in an alliance? I thought I put the position of this party very clearly before the house yesterday. We believe that we should renegotiate Canada's defence and foreign policies with an understanding as to our future role. Does the hon. member deny Canada's right to establish its own defence and foreign policies.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with some interest to some of the remarks made today. Some of the arguments such as those put forward by the speaker who preceded me in respect of savings resulting from unification are absolutely amazing. Some of the figures he used to bolster his arguments are indeed surprising. I am reminded of the very old but true saying that figures do not lie but some liars figure. Obviously some of the hon. members opposite have had access to the services of some very expert liars.
National Defence Act Amendment

speechtext: In view of the statement of the hon. member I think I am entitled to a specific reference to those figures referred to by the hon. member.

The figures themselves do not matter much. They have been quoted so many times and in so many ways I am sure they will be misleading to anyone who reads Hansard. They are bound to be confusing, though I venture to say much stress will be placed on them. Obviously it is part of the Liberal game to confuse the issue. The evidence presented before the committee is clear. If there is to be any saving, it will result from integration. The evidence is also clear that no saving will be achieved through unification.
The minister has continually said that integration and unification mean the same thing. Obviously the evidence shows that they are separate and distinct in time and in character. They are not interdependent. If we want to get that distinction clear in our minds the question as to whether integration will or will not save money becomes unimportant. The only question before us whether unification is good or bad. Obviously from the evidence unification standing by itself is of little value.
Let me remind hon. members of the evidence given before the committee regarding the limitation on savings which could be effected through integration. Late in the evening of February 21 Air Vice Marshal Hendrick, who was in charge of Canada's air defence until his retirement in 1964, appeared as a witness before the committee. I had a lengthy question to ask the air vice marshal, but because of the limitation of time I summed it up as follows, at page 1477 of the proceedings:
I have IX minutes to 10:30 and I would like to thank the air vice marshal for pointing out one thing today that people seem to have lost sight of,
14634	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment and that is in the search for economy-trying to cut down on administration costs when they seem to be rising-integration is not the only solution; that there are in fact co-operative ways which were described which did have an effect this way. Mr. Hendrick then said "Right". In other words, he adopted what I tried to sum up as his evidence, that the amount of savings which could be effected through integration was very limited, particularly to the command support services. I want to say now unreservedly that all of us in this house have every reason, even though all of us might not agree with his views, to have confidence in the capacity of the Minister of National Defence, in his credibility and his integrity.

First as to his capacity, we will be able to quote some more statements he has made. The minister himself has shown his incapacity so often that it hardly needs a comment. As to his credibility, I have always believed that the test of this is can he be believed, based on the source of his knowledge, his general sagacity, how reliable his advisers are, and so on, but general believabil-ity. Certainly no one in this house is going to
