believe a thing that the Minister of National Defence says unless they can see it proven three or four different ways, because we have seen so often that he just cannot be believed in anything.
Then as to his integrity. While I find nothing whatsoever to say for his credibility and feel that I must try very hard to say that we have some belief in his integrity, I am afraid that the consistent policy shown by the minister, and the consistent attitude of his supporters both in the defence committee and this house-that consistent policy being to make sure that the facts were not brought to the attention of the public and to try to hide the facts from this house and make sure they are not available-together with the fact that everything the minister tells us we find is not so, leaves a very serious doubt that he has any integrity at all.

When we see the actual situation to be that the minister has limited or no capacity, that the minister has no credibility, and that we have to search very diligently to find any reason to suspect that he has any integrity, we can understand why I felt that the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs was pure effrontery when he said that all of us in this house have confidence in the Minister of National Defence in this regard. If there is anyone in the house who really thinks I am being a little hard on the minister, all he has to do is look at the opening words of the Minister of National Defence himself on page 14429 of Hansard, the right-hand column. Every opportunity has been afforded those who are opposed to this concept to make their views known.

I suppose this was an opportunity afforded them, because once they are fired and their retirement leave is over, they may have the chance to open their mouths. I suppose in that way we can say this minister has afforded them the opportunity. If we are to interpret his words in that manner, I suppose we may have some faith in his credibility. If that is what he means by credibility, and that is his standard of integrity, perhaps we can go along with that a little.
April 6, 1967

I find it hard to be as charitable about his action with regard to Admiral Landymore's testimony, when he went to the extent of tampering with the evidence of a witness to make sure that we did not get the facts. That action is hardly consistent with saying:
Every opportunity has been afforded those who are opposed to this concept to make their views known.

Business of the House
party, the manner in which the defence committee was run, and the attitude of several members in this house. TRANSPORT-PROPOSED REDUCTION IN RAILWAY SERVICE BETWEEN QUEBEC AND SHERBROOKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 16 last, I had the opportunity to put the following question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill):
Has the minister received protests against the elimination of passenger trains Nos. 1, 2 and 4 between Quebec and Sherbrooke and is it his intention, in the public interest, to recommend that the Quebec Central Railway reconsider its decision.
I am pleased tonight to make the following comments on my question. On Monday, March 6,	1967, the Board of Transport
Commissioners for Canada issued order No. 123,654 relating to the application by the Quebec Central Railway Company for authorization to discontinue operation of trains Nos. 1, 2 and 4 between Quebec and Sherbrooke in the province of Quebec.
14637
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Mr. Speaker, the reasons given by the Quebec Central Railway Company and accepted by the Board of Transport Commissioners go against the public interest in a wide area and do not reflect adequately the tactics used by that company to get rid of that branch line and fail seriously in discharging its obligations toward the public.
Here are the facts:
1.	Practically all the localities served by those trains are against their being discontinued.
2.	The line on which those trains travel covers a distance of 147.6 miles between Sherbrooke and Quebec city. The industrial centres served by those trains include Sherbrooke, East Angus, Bishopton, Weedon, Saint-Gerard, Black Lake, Dark Lake, Disraeli, Coleraine, Thetford Mines, Robertson, East Broughton, Vallee Jonction, Sainte-Marie, Scott Jonction, Ville-Lambert, Breaky-ville, Charny and Quebec city.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
3.	The Quebec Central Railway Company has claimed that the average number of passengers carried on trains 1, 2 and 4 on each trip has fallen off gradually from 68 in 1962 to 26 in 1966. The communities served by this passenger train service represent a population of approximately 65,000, excluding Quebec and Sherbrooke.
The main points submitted by the Quebec Central Railway Company before the Board of Transport Commissioners to cancel the train service are as follows; first, the company reports an annual loss of $54,000; they show a reduction of passenger traffic as I have noted; and finally, they have cited the principle according to which financial loss is taken into consideration as regards the inconvenience caused to the public by abandonment of the operation.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I must say tonight in this house that the Quebec Central Railway Company, a subsidiary of the Canadian Pacific, hid the truth from the Board of Transport Commissioners and the Canadian public, since the company has increased its passenger rates which are now double those of the C.N.R. and the best way to reduce passenger traffic is for this company to increase, to double their rates, compared to the Canadian National operating in the same areas.
In addition, that company encouraged a quite unsatisfactory passenger service, often delaying train arrivals and giving traffic priority to freight trains.
We found that on the Quebec city-Sherbrooke route, for at least three years, the

14638	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion company made every effort to discourage the public from travelling on its trains, by giving preference to junction lines and freight trains, rather than passenger trains.
Finally, the said company has utterly neglected both in the area between Quebec city and Sherbrooke and throughout the province of Quebec, to promote its publicity, in order to discourage passengers from using its railway service.
The minister should intervene and advise the company to maintain its passenger service, to reduce its rates and to increase its publicity in that area.
Trains 1, 2 and 4, operating between Sherbrooke and Quebec city, must be maintained:
(a)	Passenger service, Mr. Speaker, affords better security to the public than motor vehicles.
(b)	Before deciding upon a location, industries inquire whether there is a railway service to the area.
And surely the whole region between Sherbrooke and Quebec city, through East Angus, Thetford Mines and the other municipalities I mentioned earlier in my speech, need an industrial economic development.
(c)	Even if the railway company has a deficit, it can easily be off-set by profits made elsewhere.
In closing, I would also ask the minister or his representative, or his parliamentary secretary, to bear in mind that, at the time of the centennial and Expo, over 200,000 citizens of the province of Quebec will be denied adequate railway service from Quebec city, Thetford Mines and the other municipalities, via Sherbrooke, to go and enjoy the pleasures which the centennial celebrations and the marvelous displays of Expo will offer.
I must say here, with the required emphasis, that the Canadian Pacific, through its subsidiary Quebec Central Railway, does not fulfil the obligations to which it was committed when it obtained its charter, that is to serve the public and give adequate rail service for the transportation of passengers and goods. For several years now, the Canadian Pacific has been accumulating profits to the detriment of Canadian passengers. It invests its benefits not fundamentally and primarily with a view to fulfilling its obligations as purveyor of adequate railroad services,, but rather for various reasons contrary to the

DEBATES	April 6, 1967
objectives originally agreed upon, and more specifically that of serving the public.
We see that the Canadian Pacific is building motels and launching all kinds of undertakings. Now, if the Department of Transport and the hon. minister do not intervene in this particular instance, we will soon see the company which is nourished and maintained by public taxes and government assistance, swerve completely from the course it should follow with regard to serving the public.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: FINANCE-DRUGS-INQUIRY AS TO REMOVAL OF SALES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the budget speech of two years ago, made on April 26, 1965, by the then minister of finance, the present President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon), this statement found at page 439 of Hansard for that date was made about the sales tax on drugs:
There has been much concern expressed about the high prices of drugs in Canada and proposals made that they should be exempt from the sales tax, which has always applied to them. The government has considered these representations but does not wish to act on them until the matter has been considered by the special Committee of the House on Food and Drugs.
There was an interruption at that point to which the minister replied. He then went on to say:
If the Committee comes to the conclusion that, as part of a comprehensive and effective program to reduce the prices of drugs, they should be exempt from the sales tax, I would expect to see this done in a special statute covering all the measures required to give effect to the program, and I am quite sure the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley), who is Chairman of this Committee, will see it proceeds with this very important matter just as expeditiously as it can.
April 6, 1967	COMMONS
That statement, as I say, was made two years ago in the budget speech of that year.
One year ago, as recorded in Hansard for March 29, 1966, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) renewed the undertaking given by the former minister in these words, which I quote from page 3387 of Hansard for that date:
I renew the undertaking given last year by my predecessor, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon), that if the considerations of the special committee of the house on food and drugs lead it to recommend that drugs should be exempt from sales tax as part of a comprehensive and effective program to reduce the prices of drugs, then the government would be prepared to recommend such action by means of a special statute covering all the measures required to give effect to such a program.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
It was on the basis of those two commitments that I put a question to the Minister of Finance on Tuesday, April 4, as reported at page 14485 of Hansard. I asked the minister whether in the light of these commitments and in the light of the recommendation by the special committee which has dealt with drugs and drug prices we might expect the promised legislation soon. The minister's reply was to the effect that he had been reviewing the statements made on those previous occasions and that it would be the intention of the government to proceed to remove the sales tax on drugs as part of an over-all effort to reduce the price of drugs. When I asked whether we might expect to have this legislation introduced during the present session his answer was an expression of hope.
It would be unfair of me to say that the minister's answer was unsatisfactory, but I am a little concerned about the open doors which seem to be left in these assurances which have been given to us on several occasions. There are not only the two commitments made in the budget speeches of a year and two years ago, but on several occasions in answer to questions both ministers assured the house that if the special committee made a recommendation calling for the removal of the sales tax from drugs, action to that effect would be taken.
But there is always a qualification. For one, it is to be part of an over-all package. Another qualification, of course, is that the government wishes to take action in a way which will have the desired effect, namely the lowering of the prices of drugs to consumers.
I do not quarrel with these conditions but I am concerned lest the desire to cross all the 23033-9261
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion t's and dot all the i's may result in this matter being put off as so many things are put off by the government across the way.
Surely this question has been under study by the finance department during the two years in which it has been before the committee. There has been time to think about it, and if the minister is as convinced as I felt he was by what he said on Tuesday that action must be taken with regard to this subject, I hope this action will be taken soon. I recognize that the parliamentary program always presents a problem to the government of the day, but it does seem to me that this is a very important recommendation which the special committee has made and that in the light of the firm commitments given by two ministers of finance this is a matter which ought to be dealt with expeditiously; I do not think it is good enough to leave it until next session.
The minister still has one other piece of budgetary legislation to put through this session, the one having to do with the 5 per cent refundable tax. Here is something which is, I suggest, more important. The view of the committee has been made clear: The prices of drugs are too high for the Canadian people. I hope that action on this matter can be taken soon. This is my reason for placing this subject on the list for a late show-so that I might prod the minister into doing as soon as possible something which I dare to believe he really wants to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCE-DRUGS-INQUIRY AS TO REMOVAL OF SALES TAX
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has made another fervent appeal for the removal of the sales tax on drugs. It is impossible of course for a minister of finance to forecast tax changes. I can only repeat the assurance I have given, perhaps in a somewhat different form, which may bring some comfort to the hon. member, to the house and to the country at large. The government is interested in seeing that the prices of drugs in this country are reduced.
The government will not hesitate to remove the tax as part of a program to that effect. Needless to say-and I am sure the hon. gentleman who has asked this question will agree-the removal of that tax should be used to give as much leverage as possible to other desirable action by the drug companies to bring about a reduction in the price of drugs to the consumers themselves. It is not sufficient, it seems to me, simply to remove the tax and hope for the best. I believe it ought

HISTORIC SITES AND MONUMENTS- LOUISBOURG FORTRESS-RETURN TO WORK OF MEN LAID OFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last I directed a question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing) in respect of the lay-offs at the Louisbourg project. I then referred the matter for debate on the adjournment motion, and on Monday evening the minister took it upon himself to go into the details of the problem I had placed before him. He reviewed the history for my benefit. I did not need to have the history in respect of the initiation of this project brought to my attention. I was aware that it had been carried out on the recommendation of Mr. Justice Rand and had been initiated under the Conservative government.
With the knowledge of what had taken place at that time and how this had developed I drew to the attention of the minister the fact that this has been the only effort made by any government to meet the emergency situation in respect of employment in Cape Breton. Government members like to refer to the fact that a coastguard college was established as an emergency measure, but I should like to point out that this was very meaningless because it followed the closing of a naval base by the same government. Assistance by this government in respect of the economy or the employment situation in Cape Breton has been lacking in many ways.
The minister never got around to answering my question. He said that the salaries had been increased by 50 per cent. That means that the men who are employed there still are almost 50 per cent below the prevailing rates. The increase of 50 per cent still leaves the workers at Louisbourg far below the average wage earners in the Cape Breton area. The minister said that he did think the men could work for a rate of $1.09 an hour. I should like to ask him whether he has made similar adjustments in the salaries of other northern affairs workers throughout the rest of the country, because these men in Louisbourg are still receiving more than some men in other areas. I am not suggesting that this is a justification for the low rate paid at Louisbourg.
The minister also said that this past year, in response to representations made by his colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), 44 men were taken on again. Forty four men were taken on after

DEBATES	April 6, 1967
a lay-off of approximately 150 men. As I understand it these men were not taken on as new employees at the project, but were men who were returned to their work as a result of having been laid off a few days earlier. Therefore, in response to a request by his colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the minister did not hire 44 men. All the minister did was take back on the job the men who had been laid off. This is an old Liberal trick-slash here and slash there, and then take them back and make heroes of themselves.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
Nothing has been done to assist the economy of Cape Breton by any government since the Louisbourg project was initiated by the Conservative government. Let me call the minister's attention to what he said, as reported at page 14471 of Hansard for April 3, 1967:
We have exhausted the money. We exhausted it on March 31, and we have laid off 44 men.
Thirteen lines later he said:
We are keeping relatively within our costs, hut I want to have something produced.
We all want to have something produced, but why should there be a cutback on the Louisbourg project in that part of the country where unemployment is so high?
Last November the government said there was no more money for the winter works program. The Minister of Labour and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration have repeatedly said that the only alteration to the winter works program was the discontinuance of the $500 bonus paid in respect of winter housing starts. These have nothing to do with the Louisbourg project. Let me remind the minister that some of his colleagues have indicated that winter works projects can be done as well in the winter as in the summer. We now have a denial of this, for the convenience of a minister.
There have been 44 men laid off on this particular project because, as is suggested, this work cannot be done during the wintertime. That is in direct contradiction to what has been said by other ministers on other occasions. Has there been any cutback during the winter here in Ottawa in respect of the arts centre? Originally it was to cost some $12 million. The government is still pouring money into this project and I understand the cost has now increased to about $15 million. Expo started out to be a $20 million project and I understand it is now to cost in the
April 6, 1967
neighbourhood of $100 million. Let us remember the $10 million to be spent on the film industry.
This minister has said the money so far as the Louisbourg project is concerned has been exhausted. If money is to be spent by this government so easily in respect of the arts centre and Expo I suggest that additional money can be found for Cape Breton.

Most of the men were miners, and with that meticulous care that they have down there, a certain number of them had to come from one little village, a specific number from another, and so many from Sydney, and we had to carry them down by bus.

As to the prevailing rates, for every increase in pay that we gave to these men we had representations from the industry in the area that we pay our men too much and are affecting their industry.
